title: Radii of Sn Isotopes near the Proton Dripline from Nuclear Lattice Effective Field Theory
abstract: We present the first $\textit{ab initio}$ lattice calculations of charge and matter radii of tin isotopes $^{96}$Sn, $^{98}$Sn, $^{100}$Sn, $^{102}$Sn and $^{104}$Sn near the proton dripline using nuclear lattice effective field theory with high-fidelity two- and three-nucleon forces combined with the partial-pinhole algorithm. The resulting radii are larger then predicted from other ab-initio methods. We find that variations of the three-nucleon interaction reveal substantial radius differences even among interactions with similar binding energies. We intensively discuss of the role of different choices of the three-body forces.

title: Lepton $g-2$ non-universality of hadronic contributions and a sub-GeV window to New Physics
abstract: We propose the linear combination of the anomalous magnetic moments of the muon and electron, $a_{\mu-e} \equiv a_\mu - (m_\mu/m_e)^2 a_e$, as a natural low-energy window quantity that may directly probe the current discrepancy between the data-driven and lattice-QCD evaluations of hadronic contributions. The rescaling ensures an exact cancellation of the leading short-range ($m_\ell^2$-scaling) effects, thereby improving the UV behavior. Because entire classes of contributions cancel identically --- not merely in variance --- the combination is predictable in chiral perturbation theory with no free low-energy constant, and it isolates flavor-non-universal New Physics. The hadronic-vacuum-polarization effect in $a^{\rm HVP}_{\mu-e}$, together with its uncertainty, is reduced as compared to $a^{\rm HVP}_{\mu}$ by $\sim 85\%$. This is promising for tests of New Physics with some degree of flavor non-universality, conditional on significant improvements in the measurements of $a_e$ and $\alpha$.

title: Bogoliubov self-consistent $GW$ and second-order Green's function methods for attractive fermionic interactions
abstract: Describing fermionic systems with attractive interactions, such as superconductors and atomic nuclei, beyond the mean-field level remains a central challenge. In this work, we investigate the performance of Bogoliubov fully self-consistent $GW$ (Bog.~sc$GW$) and second-order Green's function (Bog.~scGF2) methods, implemented within a unified imaginary-time and imaginary-frequency framework. Using two attractive Hubbard lattices ($4\times4$ and $2\times8$) as a model study and benchmarking against full configuration interaction (FCI), we find that, for these systems, Bog.~scGF2 provides a more accurate description than Bog.~sc$GW$. In particular, Bog.~sc$GW$ systematically overestimates the correlation energy, with errors increasing rapidly as the attractive interaction strength grows. These results suggest the importance of exchange contributions in such strongly correlated fermionic systems, even when exchange effects are included only at low order in perturbation theory.

From Multimessenger Inference to Simulations: A Ranked Ensemble of Finite-Temperature Equations of State
abstract: We construct a set of microphysical, finite-temperature equations of state (EOSs) for numerical simulations of neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae that is consistent with modern constraints from nuclear theory and multimessenger astronomy and systematically spans the posterior distribution of allowed EOSs. The EOSs are based on a simplified Skyrme functional whose inputs are nuclear matter saturation properties, extended to supra-saturation densities through the speed of sound at a set of reference densities. The models are assigned continuous likelihood weights from chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations, the gravitational-wave signal GW170817, and four NICER mass-radius measurements. From the resulting catalog of 3.6 million EOSs, the posterior yields $R_{1.4} = 11.8^{+0.8}_{-0.7}$ km, $\Lambda_{1.4} = 342^{+181}_{-118}$, and $M_{\rm max}^{\rm TOV} = 2.17^{+0.23}_{-0.16}\,M_\odot$ (medians with 90% credible intervals). From this posterior we select a ranked twelve-member ensemble, headed by a fiducial, central EOS, whose members are individually plausible while bracketing the posterior spread of each neutron-star observable. For all ensemble members we generate general-purpose finite-temperature tables with the SROEOS code, each accompanied by nucleon effective-mass variants for systematic studies of thermal effects, to be made publicly available upon publication.

title: Performance and damage mechanisms of dispersion-strengthened tungsten under H-mode plasma in DIII-D
abstract: Abstract Dispersion strengthened tungsten (DSW) alloys are promising materials for plasma facing components, displaying improved mechanical properties and microstructure stability compared to pure tungsten. In this work, the performance of DSW reinforced with 1 wt% transition-metal carbide (TaC, TiC, or ZrC) has been examined under H-mode plasma in the DIII-D tokamak. DSW samples were mounted both flush with the divertor floor and at a 10 ∘ angle towards the incoming plasma fluxes to further increase the heat and particle loading. To simulate the impact of prolonged tokamak operation, similar plasma exposures were repeated on two additional sets of DSW samples: one set pre-implanted with 10 22 m − 2 helium, and another set heated in-situ to an additional 500 ∘ C. Flush mounted samples exhibited good surface stability, with no evidence of melting or cracking regardless of composition or treatment. Carbon redeposition was observed on most samples, likely due to the graphite environment of DIII-D. Under coupled thermal loading and helium implantation, surface nanostructuring developed in some DSW samples; however, DSW containing tantalum dispersion phases showed strong resistance to such surface modification. In contrast, obvious surface melting was observed on 10 ∘ angled samples containing TaC and ZrC dispersoids, likely associated with dispersoid oxidation during fabrication, which reduced thermal conductivity and promoted elevated surface temperatures during plasma exposure. The grain morphology of DSW containing TiC remained largely unchanged, although near-surface dispersoids on the angled TiC sample were missing after plasma exposure. The loss is associated with oxidation of the dispersoids during fabrication, followed by sublimation during plasma exposure. Through systematic comparison of DSW performance under H mode plasma conditions, this study identifies key degradation mechanisms and highlights strategies to improve the performance of DSW as plasma facing materials.

title: First experimental observation of ‘Staircase’ high confinement mode in tokamak plasma
abstract: Abstract In magnetically confined nuclear fusion, the achievement of ignition necessitates the tokamak plasma in a high confinement state known as H-mode. A major challenge encountered in the standard H-mode is the abrupt collapse of its ultrathin edge layer. Here, we report a first experimental demonstration that a stable H-mode can be sustained by a staircase plasma profile. The basic physical picture is: by staircasing the plasma profile, the potential free energy stored in one single large edge layer is distributed into multiple mesoscale layers throughout the entire plasma volume. Consequently, the large scale edge collapse is converted into small scale desynchronized fluctuations, effectively reducing the risk of violent relaxation event. This finding uncovers a new benign high confinement regime of the tokamak plasma.

title: Experimental characterization of thin-foil heating by counter-propagating kJ-class ultra-intense laser
abstract: Abstract In fast-ignition laser fusion, understanding high-density plasma heating driven bypicosecond ultra-intense lasers is essential. Thin-foil heating under counter irradiation wasexperimentally characterized using the kilojoule-class picosecond LFEX laser, and theassociated experimental constraints were clarified. Counter-irradiation was realized viaplasma-mirror-based beam steering, and a comparison between 90-degree and 180-degreereflection configurations showed that the 180-degree configuration enablescounter-irradiation at intensities exceeding 10$^{18}$ W/cm$^2$. Cu and Ti doped deuterated polystyrene thin foil were developed to allow simultaneous measurements of electrontemperature and fusion reactions. In counter-illumination experiments using planarthin-foil targets, Beam-fusion reactions driven by counter-streaming fast ions wereobserved; however, the electron temperature remained around 2 keV, comparable toone-sided irradiation. In contrast, one-sided irradiation combining pulse cleaning andlaser-guiding-cone focusing achieved an electron temperature of 10 keV. These resultsindicate that, at intensities on the order of 10$^{18}$ W/cm$^2$, high contrast and enhancedfocusing are required for effective plasma heating.

title: Edge ion heat flux as a key parameter of the L-H transition: insights from ion and electron heating experiments on TCV
abstract: Abstract We investigate the role of the edge ion heat flux $Q_\mathrm{i,edge}$ in the L--H transition on TCV, comparing purely electron-heated (ECRH) and dominantly ion-heated (low-energy NBI) plasmas. The two heating schemes produce different $P_\mathrm{L-H}$ trends. ECRH discharges exhibit the characteristic non-monotonic density dependence, while NBI discharges show a monotonically increasing power threshold with values up to three times lower at comparable densities. However, when expressed in terms of the edge ion heat flux, both datasets show a monotonic density dependence even at low density, where the electron--ion collisional energy exchange is inefficient, suggesting that the ion heat flux, not the total loss power, plays a key role in the physics of the L--H transition. These results extend the critical edge ion heat flux criterion to a carbon-wall device and to dominantly ion-heated conditions, and support $Q_\mathrm{i,edge}$-based approaches as a physics-grounded complement to conventional $P_\mathrm{L-H}$ scalings.

title: Characterization of a novel disruption mechanism during plasma current ramp-down in the ADITYA-U tokamak
abstract: Abstract Safe termination of a tokamak plasma discharge remains a challenge due to the high risk of encountering a magnetohydrodynamic (MHD)-driven disruption during controlled ramp-down of the plasma current. During the current ramp-down phase of ADITYA-U discharges, the occurrence of MHD-driven disruptions cannot be described by the conventional locked-mode disruption (LMD) mechanism. Analysing hundreds of ADITYA-U discharges, it has been observed that when some specific plasma parameters exceeds a threshold rate, the disruption is always preceded by a steady rise in MHD mode-rotation frequency, followed by a sudden cessation of mode-rotation frequency before the current quench. Moreover, it has been found that the occurrence of this type of disruption depends mainly on the current decay rate and magnitude and the edge safety factor (qedge). Although the disruption seems to be predominantly governed only by the m/n=2/1 drift–tearing modes, the precursor phase in this kind of disruption survives for relatively much shorter times as compared to the conventional locked mode disruptions. Further investigation revealed that during the plasma current decay phase, the core radiation increases significantly, indicating a hollow temperature profile. This leads to destabilization of the MHD mode, which seems to be primarily responsible for the plasma disruption.

title: A magnetostatic shield for the RF driver: impact on the plasma properties & extraction performance of the ITER Negative IonSource
abstract: Abstract The experimental fusion reactor ITER relies on neutral beam injectors as auxiliary heating system, providing 33 MW of heating power to the fusion plasma. ITER neutral beams are obtained through neutralisation of negative ion hydrogen/deuterium beams accelerated up to 1 MeV. The ion source consists of an inductively coupled plasma powered by radio-frequency (RF) generators, where a magnetic filter field is necessary to lower electron temperature and density in the extraction region, minimizing the destruction of negative ions. However, an excessive filter field in the driver region was found to limit the RF coupling, motivating the investigation of a magnetostatic shield placed around the RF drivers to screen stray magnetic fields and reduce the filter field effect on the driver plasma, without compromising electron filtering in the extraction region.This work presents a plasma characterization study of the magnetostatic shield effect, tested at SPIDER and MINION, two test facilities hosted at Consorzio RFX in Padova (Italy) within the Neutral Beam Test Facility (NBTF). Results from SPIDER are discussed, focusing on plasma properties measured with Langmuir probes and optical emission spectroscopy, supported by a Collisional Radiative (CR) model. It is shown that the extracted negative ion current density is nearly unaffected by the shield, even at high filter field values, while a wider range of plasma grid currents becomes accessible without left-right asymmetry in the RF driver pairs.

title: The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter of the ePIC detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is a next-generation facility expected to address fundamental open questions in nuclear physics, including the structure and dynamics of gluons in nucleons and nuclei. The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC) is the electromagnetic calorimeter of the ePIC detector, designed to meet the stringent performance requirements of the EIC, providing precise measurements and particle identification of scattered electrons, photons, and neutral mesons. The BIC is a high-granularity sampling calorimeter based on lead absorbers interleaved with scintillating fibers, complemented by pixelated imaging layers based on the AstroPix monolithic active pixel sensor. This hybrid design enables both accurate energy and position measurements, as well as three-dimensional shower reconstruction, making it a key component for realizing the full physics potential of the EIC. The BIC has successfully completed its Preliminary Design Review last year and is currently progressing toward the Final Design Review. In this talk, I will present an overview of the BIC concept and focus on its current status and performance results from bench tests, system integration studies, and recent beam tests.
authors: for the ePIC Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC)

title: The ALICE asynchronous software trigger processing for LHC Run 3
abstract: The detector and computing upgrades for LHC Run 3 enable ALICE to continuously acquire proton--proton (pp) and lead--lead (Pb--Pb) collisions at interaction rates of up to 1.5 MHz and 50 kHz, respectively. The resulting pp dataset is more than three orders of magnitude larger than the combined Run 1 and Run 2 samples, and its long-term retention in full would be impractical given the available storage capacity. To address this challenge, ALICE has implemented a physics-driven asynchronous software trigger designed to retain only collisions containing signals of physics interest. Following full asynchronous reconstruction, the Central Event Filter Processor applies more than 100 analysis-based selection channels spanning the ALICE pp physics programme. The selected collisions are then used to skim the original Compressed Time Frames (CTFs), preserving the relevant detector information within detector-specific time windows. This procedure reduces the retained CTF volume to approximately 4.5% of its original size, while preserving the possibility of future reconstruction with improved calibrations and software. This contribution describes the implementation and operation of the asynchronous software trigger, from collision selection to CTF skimming, and highlights how this strategy provides access to rare signals and processes across the ALICE physics programme.
authors: Sara Pucillo for the ALICE Collaboration

title: Projected Sensitivity of a Differential Torsion Sensor for Tests of the Weak Equivalence Principle
abstract: Tests of the weak equivalence principle (WEP) are among the most sensitive probes of new long-range, composition-dependent interactions beyond general relativity and the Standard Model. We evaluate the potential of a differential torsion sensor, which combines long mechanical coherence times with optical-cavity readout and common-mode rejection, for laboratory WEP tests and fifth-force searches. For a representative configuration based on an existing prototype, with Be-Ti test masses and 180 days of coherent integration, the projected noise-limited sensitivity to the E\"otv\"os parameter is $\eta\simeq7.5\times10^{-16}$ and $2.4\times10^{-16}$ for signal modulation at 2 and 20 mHz, respectively, below current ground-based torsion-balance limits. For a baryon-coupled Yukawa interaction sourced by the Earth, the corresponding projected sensitivity to the coupling strength is $\alpha\simeq3.1\times10^{-13}$ and $9.8\times10^{-14}$ for ranges $\lambda\gtrsim10^{7}$ m. We identify the modulation scheme, the material contrast, and the source geometry as the main factors that set the projected reach, and the control of systematic couplings as the main experimental requirement for attaining it. These results indicate that differential torsion sensors are a promising platform for future laboratory WEP tests.

title: Producing $\mu$Bq/m3-level low-226Ra ultrapure water for the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory
abstract: The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20 kton low-background liquid-scintillator (LS) detector, was designed primarily to determine the neutrino mass ordering. JUNO requires ultrapure water (UPW) with a Ra concentration < 50~$\mu$Bq/m3 because of the direct liquid-liquid contact between LS and UPW during detector filling. To meet this stringent requirement, a high-sensitivity measurement system capable of detecting Ra in water down to 3.9 $\mu$Bq/m3 was developed, and the 100 t/h UPW production process was optimized. By integrating selective ion-exchange resin with membrane-based separation technologies, the system consistently produced UPW with a Ra concentration of <4$\mu$Bq/m3, exceeding the JUNO specification and, to our knowledge, representing one of the lowest reported levels achieved at this engineering scale. This paper describes the design and implementation of JUNO's UPW system and the high-sensitivity Ra measurement platform, together with a systematic evaluation of Ra removal efficiencies across the purification train and validation of the final water quality.

title: Interferometry radii at RHIC BES energies within the integrated HydroKinetic model
abstract: The work is devoted to research of pion femtoscopic correlations in relativistic heavy-ion collisions across the RHIC Beam Energy Scan range using the extended integrated HydroKinetic Model (iHKMe). The model provides a comprehensive description of the system’s dynamical evolution, starting from the initial collision state of colliding nuclei, passing through a possible thermalization process and hydrodynamic expansion to the hadron interacting cascade and formation of the observed particle spectra. The model smoothly couples all these stages of the matter evolution, ensuring a smooth transition between the stages. A primary focus of the current work, in contrast to the similar investigation within iHKM for high energies, concentrated in the energy region where extended nuclear overlap times and incomplete thermalization significantly influence the system’s expansion comparing with very high energies. We extract the three-dimensional interferometry radii ( $$R_{\text {out}}$$ , $$R_{\text {side}}$$ , $$R_{\text {long}}$$ ) in the region from 7.7 to 39 GeV per nucleon pair and evaluate their sensitivity to the features of the equation of state (EoS), specifically comparing crossover and first-order phase transition scenarios. The model demonstrates good agreement with experimental measurements in the crossover case. As for the first-order phase transition scenario, the $$R_{\text {long}}$$ component, at the optimal model parameters for particle spectra, is noticeably higher than the experimental data, and the difference is more pronounced with the growth of collision energy. Such a behavior is caused by the increased system’s lifetime during the mixed-phase stage. The corresponding analysis within iHKMe below $$\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 7.7$$ GeV will be presented within a separate investigation.

title: Characterization of the fast neutron response of liquid scintillator detectors at NFS
abstract: The fast neutron response of MONSTER and sTED liquid scintillation detectors was investigated using time-of-flight measurements at the Neutrons For Science facility at GANIL-SPIRAL2. A continuous neutron beam produced by 40 MeV deuterons on a thick beryllium converter was used to obtain pulse height distributions for selected incident neutron energies. Digital pulse shape analysis was used to distinguish neutron-induced events and reduce pile-up effects. For MONSTER, the response and detection efficiency were studied up to 40 MeV using Geant4 with previously obtained light output functions and PHITS in SCINFUL mode. The comparison examines the increasing importance of carbon reaction channels and the divergence between the calculated efficiencies above 20 MeV. For sTED, light output functions for recoil deuterons and alpha particles were determined for the first time for this detector. The measured and calculated efficiencies were compared up to 20 MeV. The sTED efficiency shows a good overall agreement with the simulations. These results provide experimentally constrained detector response information for nuclear data measurements and identify limitations that must be considered when extending the simulations to higher neutron energies.

title: Optimal density profiles for phase-locked laser-wakefield acceleration
abstract: Laser-wakefield accelerators support extremely high accelerating fields, but dephasing, arising from the subluminal group velocity of the driving laser, limits both energy gain and laser-to-beam efficiency. Plasma density tailoring can mitigate dephasing, but determining the required profile in the nonlinear regime relevant to current experiments remains challenging. Here, we present a method to compute the density profile required for phase-locked laser-wakefield acceleration (LWFA) using a lightweight closed-loop controller embedded within particle-in-cell simulations. Complementary analytical expressions for the nonlinear regime predict that phase-locking can increase electron energies by up to a factor of 2, although quantitative accuracy requires a numerical approach to account for the spectral-temporal evolution of the laser pulse. Phase-locked simulations approximately double both the final energy and laser-to-beam efficiency relative to constant-density cases. These results demonstrate that density-tailored phase-locking is a practical route to efficient LWFA stages operating up to the depletion limit.

title: Study of the intra-pixel timing resolution of planar silicon sensors using the TDCpix ASIC
abstract: A study of the intra-pixel timing resolution in planar silicon detectors, bonded to the TDCpix Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), is performed using the TimePix4 telescope. Spatial non-uniformities in the timing resolution, arising from the weighting field, are measured for the first time in an experimental environment. The results are validated using simulation and discussed in the context of future Research and Development (R&D) goals.

title: Simulation Study of the MPD Performance for Dielectron Measurements at NICA
abstract: The Multi-Purpose Detector (MPD) experiment at NICA is designed to investigate strongly interacting matter at high net-baryon density through a broad program of heavy-ion measurements. Dielectrons constitute one of the key probes in this program, with contributions emitted throughout the entire space-time evolution of the collision. Their experimental measurement is, however, challenged by a large combinatorial background arising primarily from incompletely reconstructed photon conversions and Dalitz decays of light neutral mesons. In this work, we study the expected performance and capabilities of the MPD experiment for dielectron measurements using simulated minimum-bias $^{209}$Bi+$^{209}$Bi collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 9.2 GeV. Electron identification is performed using the combined information from the TPC, the TOF detector and the ECal. A previously developed multilayer-perceptron classifier is used for electron identification, providing a substantial increase in electron detection efficiency relative to sequential one-dimensional selections while preserving an electron-sample purity close to unity. To address the dominant sources of combinatorial background, a pair-analysis strategy is developed that exploits partially reconstructed electron tracks. The method combines the pair opening angle, the TPC dE/dx signal, and an approximate reconstruction of the pair invariant mass to tag tracks from photon conversions and $\pi^0$ Dalitz decays at the pair level. In the mass interval 0.2 $< m_{ee}<0.7 $ GeV/$c^2$, the method improves the signal-to-background ratio by a factor of about 3.5 with the current track reconstruction algorithm. The study demonstrates the strong potential of the MPD experiment for dielectron measurements at NICA energies and highlights the importance of further improvements in low-$p_{\rm T}$ track reconstruction.

title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
abstract: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

Graphene Transfer for Vertical Amorphous-Selenium Photodetectors: Fabrication, Optical Transmission and Operation at 77 K
abstract: Graphene can serve as a VUV transparent electrode in vertical photodetector devices. Using an optically transparent graphene as a top-electrode of amorphous selenium (a-Se) photoconductor requires transfer process compatible with the thermal and chemical sensitivities of a-Se thin films. The baking and polymer-removal steps of conventional commercial Trivial Transfer graphene procedures are undesirable because heating can promote selenium crystallization and prolonged solvent exposure can cause delamination. We implement two alternatives: PMMA-free transfer of nominal 50-layer graphene and transfer of nominal 10-layer graphene using an approximately 80 nm PMMA support removed in acetone at 40C. Raman G and 2D bands identify graphene after transfer. Separate graphene/MgF2 specimens are characterized by dark-corrected transmission measurements over 120-325 nm and compared with earlier single-layer and nominal 6-8-layer Trivial Transfer spectra. The completed graphene/a-Se/Cr devices produce bias-dependent voltage transients under pulsed 415 nm illumination at 293 K and 77 K. These results establish an a-Se-compatible fabrication route for graphene-electrode devices and demonstrate vertical device operation at both room and cryogenic temperatures. The completed devices provide a platform for detection-efficiency studies, and direct VUV photoresponse measurements now underway.

title: FPGA-based LQG controller and hardware-in-the-loop simulator implementation for nanomechanical systems
abstract: We present an open-source framework for real-time Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation on the affordable Red Pitaya STEMlab FPGA platform. The controller implements a discrete-time Kalman filter and Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) for systems with up to three coupled oscillatory degrees of freedom, targeting applications in levitated optomechanics, MEMS/NEMS, and related experimental platforms. Complementing the controller, the HIL simulator provides a~configurable second-order stochastic plant with nonlinear input and output mappings, enabling realistic closed-loop testing under real-time and fixed-point constraints. A MATLAB-based workflow automates model configuration, controller synthesis, numerical scaling, and FPGA deployment without requiring specialized hardware expertise. As an end-to-end demonstration, we present the stabilization of a levitated nanoparticle in a two-dimensional double-well potential, illustrating the complete workflow from model definition and simulation to real-time feedback control. The codebase: https://github.com/TU-Wien-ACIN-CDS/FPGA-based-LQG-and-HIL-simulator-for-nanomechanical-systems

title: Design and performance of the front-end readout electronics for LACT
abstract: The Large Array of Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope (LACT) will complement the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) with a target angular resolution of 0.05 degrees to resolve the morphology of Very-High-Energy gamma-ray sources. The array is designed to comprise 32 telescopes with 6-meter apertures within LHAASO at an altitude of approximately 4410 meters. Each camera contains 1616 silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). We developed a front-end readout electronics (FEE) board integrating 16 channels of SiPM gain compensation and high-speed waveform sampling for operation at high altitude and over a wide temperature range. The gain compensation circuit independently adjusts the operating voltage of each SiPM according to its temperature and monitors the actual operating voltage. Previous tests of the adopted compensation scheme showed SiPM gain drift below 2% from -20 to 30 degrees Celsius. The waveform sampling circuit uses two 14-bit AC9628 analog-to-digital converters, each operating in eight-channel mode, to digitize the SiPM pulse waveform at 250 million samples per second. The integral nonlinearity of the DC response is 0.0709% over a differential DC voltage range of -950 mV to +950 mV at the AC9628 input. Equivalent electrical pulses with a full width at half maximum of 37.42 ns are used to simulate the SiPM output signals. At a differential pulse amplitude of approximately 237 mV at the AC9628 input, the pulse integral area resolution is 0.2725%. This paper presents the circuit design and performance tests of the FEE for the LACT camera.

title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves $\sim\!300$ nm lateral and $\sim\!650$ nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and $ \!5\times$ faster volumetric acquisition (up to $3.25 \times 10^6$ voxels s$^{-1}$). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by $\sim\!2\times$ and restores volumetric resolving power by $>\!2\times$ relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

title: 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers
abstract: Electron ptychography recovers atomic structure from 4D-STEM data: diffraction patterns at multiple positions of a scanned probe. Current codes reconstruct an image and read atoms off it, or fit atoms under an $L_1$ loss; neither gives per-atom uncertainty. We propose 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits the atoms, the microscope, and the detector directly to the recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. The output is a list of atoms, each a Gaussian primitive with a 3D position, a thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar from the Fisher information. The Fisher information also conditions the solver, gives the dose (electrons per {\AA}$^2$) each parameter needs, and separates calibration from imaging. On a simulated WSe$_2$ bilayer, starting from the published reconstruction, fitted atoms cut in-plane error by a third (3.2 vs. 4.8 pm) and depth error by 40-61% against its 3D peaks. Depth comes from multiple scattering into the dark field, the faint counts outside the direct beam. The two layers, $10\times$ closer than the depth of field, separate; per-atom depth then follows the layer geometry. When the model is well specified, the bars are calibrated (69% of position coordinates within $1\sigma$). On experimental WSe$_2$, fitted atoms predict held-out patterns better than the three published codes we test. With free probe modes where atoms are incomplete, the same likelihood predicts best on all three held-out benchmarks, matches every WSe$_2$ baseline in 5 min against up to 20.5 h, and passes torchslice at its released setting 180$\times$ sooner on PrScO$_3$. Per-atom error bars, planned doses, and fast reconstruction point to low-dose, real-time 3D imaging of beam-sensitive and dynamic materials.

title: Ultraviolet emission from the $$^{229\mathrm m}$$Th isomer in neutron star mergers
abstract: Thorium in the universe is primarily synthesized via the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process), with neutron star mergers serving as an important astrophysical site for its production. In particular, the heavy nucleus $$^{229}$$ Th exhibits a unique low-energy isomeric state at 8.3 eV, giving rise to an isolated ultraviolet (UV) spectral line that has no analogue among known transitions in other heavy nuclei. In this work, we investigate the observational signatures associated with this low-lying state $$^{229\mathrm m}$$ Th in neutron star mergers. For sufficiently neutron-rich trajectories, the FRDM2012 and WS4 nuclear mass models predict comparable $$^{229}$$ Th abundances, with the isomer abundance reaches $$\sim 10^{-6}$$ for an assumed $$^{229}$$ Ac $$\beta $$ -decay feeding fraction of 14%. For the dynamical trajectory with a temperature of $$\sim 10^{4}$$ K, the effective transition rate from the low-lying state to the ground state is $$\sim 10^{-4}$$ s $$^{-1}$$ , implying an effective lifetime on the order of hours. The decay transition of $$^{229\mathrm m}$$ Th produces a distinct UV spectral feature near 1500 Å, providing a promising spectroscopic fingerprint for the direct and unambiguous identification of thorium in neutron star mergers. However, detecting UV lines remains a significant challenge with current instruments, particularly in the far-UV region at wavelengths below 2000 Å. Under the adopted ejecta and radiative transfer assumptions, the emission line would be detectable by the proposed Ultraviolet Explorer only from very nearby sources within $$\mathcal {O}(10-100)~\textrm{kpc}$$ .

title: Time-Varying Bayesian Optimization and Extremum Seekingfor Drift-Tube Linac Tuning at LANSCE
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a promising machine learning approach to accelerator tuning. It has the advantage of being able to incorporate prior information, including simulation and historical data, and explicitly model measurement noise. However, standard implementations can produce large, abrupt parameter updates that are undesirable and potentially unsafe in accelerator operation. They may also spend excessive time exploring less promising regions of the search space. We address these limitations by imposing soft and hard step size limits. We evaluate these methods by adjusting the radio frequency settings of the drift tube linac (DTL) at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE) to maximize the particle count at the end of the linac. We first test the methods in simulation with constant exogenous parameters, then repeat the tests with drifting exogenous parameters. Under drifting conditions, progressively reducing the BO step size limit improved convergence. We also find that an initial BO segment followed by extremum seeking (ES), an approach we call BO-ES, combines BO's use of prior information and sample efficiency with ES's effectiveness in local optimization and drift tracking. Finally, tests on the LANSCE accelerator with BO-ES demonstrate an approximately $25\%$ reduction in losses at the end of the linac across different configurations of historical and simulation data.

title: Comparative study of damage on tungsten materials irradiated by ELM-like plasma with different energy densities expected in ITER operations
abstract: Abstract During the operation of the tokamak device, the high heat load released by the core plasma instability events severely affects the structure and performance of tungstenbased divertor materials. For the expected Type I ELMs in future long-pulse steadystate fusion devices, the coaxial gun discharge plasma parameters are designed to simulate the characteristics of low-medium energy density. Under constant initial conditions (discharge frequency, gas-prefilled), the total accumulated heat flux is kept constant by varying the energy density and the number of pulses. By combining the plasma-material interaction process, the temperature evolution of tungsten (W) target under different heat loads and its damage effects are comparatively studied. The results show that when the total energy is fixed, the thermal deposition time scale and the instantaneous temperature gradient lead to different types of damage, including roughening, grain loss, blistering, crack networks, and cracking accompanied by melting. Low-energy-density multi-pulse impacts cause slow heat deposition and small temperature gradients, increasing surface roughness via cyclic thermal stress. Highenergy-density impacts involving only a few pulses cause rapid heat deposition and steep temperature gradients, inducing high thermal stresses that lead to blistering and cracking. The energy density of an individual pulse determines the transition from surface to bulk damage. These results suggest that peak heat load control should take priority over cumulative heat flux limitation in the service design of W targets for fusion devices.

title: The Population of Radio Hypernebulae from Mass-Transferring Massive Binaries
abstract: Massive binary evolution is punctuated by brief phases of highly super-Eddington mass transfer (MT) onto neutron stars and black holes, presaging luminous transients such as supernovae, common envelope events, and gravitational wave sources. These hyper-accreting phases power relativistic jets and slower mass-loaded outflows, inflating extended nebulae of relativistic particles. Though observed in the local universe as ultra-luminous X-ray binaries and micro-quasars, the present census is biased against shorter-lived and hence rarer but potentially even more extreme MT systems: so-called ``hypernebulae'' (HNbe). We use the binary population synthesis code (\textsc{COMPAS}) to estimate the MT population, which spans a wide range of MT rates $\dot{M} \sim 10^{2-7}\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$ and source lifetimes $t_{\rm acc} \sim 10^{0-6}$ years. Combining this synthetic population with a semi-analytic model for their time-dependent radio emission, we predict the observable properties of HNbe over cosmic time. HNbe exhibit a broad GHz luminosity range extending to $L_{\nu, \rm peak} \sim 10^{28-30}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$, and up to $\sim 10^{2}$ ($\sim 10^{5}$) HNbe are detectable by the wide-field radio surveys VLASS (DSA-2000) in our conservative model. A fraction of these systems should possess angular sizes and spatial offsets from star-forming regions (due to the first supernova kick) resolvable by VLBI. The most luminous donors, helium Hertzsprung-gap stars, may be detectable coincident with radio HNbe with Roman imaging out to distances $\sim 30$\,Mpc. Our findings suggest HNbe as promising probes of the pathways linking massive binaries to energetic transients.

title: Residual diffusion for fine-structure enhancement in low-count accelerator-based muon imaging
abstract: Accelerator-based muon imaging combines the penetrating power of high-energy muons with selectable momentum and a controlled beam direction, offering a powerful means of probing internal structures in large, dense and heavily shielded objects. Within a fixed beam-time budget, realizing this potential requires reliable recovery of fine structures from limited muon statistics. We propose an observation-conditioned residual diffusion method with decoupled linear schedules to enhance low-count muon images through iterative restoration guided by the observed image. We evaluate a simplified VSC-24 fuel cask under an idealized 5 GeV parallel muon beam, using 500,000 accepted events per low-count image and 40 million per reference image. Simulation results show improved recovery of structural boundaries and fine details, with the mean peak signal-to-noise ratio increasing from 11.4239 to 22.1719 dB. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion models to make more effective use of limited muon data and broaden the application of accelerator-based muon imaging across scientific and industrial settings.

title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics
abstract: Computational research requires repeated decisions about models, calculations and the interpretation of results. We introduce Brilliance, an agent that combines large language models, reusable physics expertise and numerical simulation to construct and revise investigations in accelerator physics. Starting from a detailed expert-specified request, Brilliance develops an ideal storage-ring lattice meeting the specified emittance ceiling and sampled nonlinear-acceptance criteria after revising optics that fail particle-tracking tests. Further scientist-guided exploration produces a candidate with a natural emittance of 6.51 pm rad and millimeter-scale transverse acceptance, while exposing unresolved momentum-acceptance limitations. Using measured responses from the High Energy Photon Source, Brilliance also performs offline optics calibration consistent with an independent specialist analysis. An expert-module ablation examines how reusable domain knowledge influences research choices and outcomes. Here, we demonstrate a practical route to scientist-agent collaboration in sustained numerical research.

title: Beam-Driven Active Plasma Dechirper for Energy Stabilization of High-Charge Bunches
abstract: Plasma-based accelerators offer ultrahigh electric field gradients, yet delivering high-charge bunches with simultaneously low energy jitter and narrow energy spread remains a critical challenge. We propose a beam-driven active plasma dechirper integrated with a magnetic chicane to suppress both imperfections. By operating in the blowout regime at low plasma density, the dechirper accommodates a stretched witness bunch, thereby mitigating beam-loading effects and preserving the linear slope of the longitudinal wakefield for precise energy stabilization. Furthermore, a tailored initial energy chirp is introduced to reconcile the disparate optimal plasma lengths required for correcting jitter and spread. Three-dimensional simulations demonstrate that for a 1~GeV, 1~nC electron bunch, this scheme simultaneously reduces the energy jitter and spread from $\pm2$\% and 1\% to $\pm0.05$\% and 0.05\%, respectively, while maintaining nearly 100\% transmission.

title: The production of lepton pairs in heavy-ion collisions at SPS and RHIC energies
abstract: We perform a quantitative study of dilepton production and elliptic flow in In+In collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=17.3$ GeV and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200$ GeV, concentrating on the low and intermediate invariant mass regions. The medium evolution is simulated event-by-event with the multistage iEBE-MUSIC framework, and the electromagnetic emission combines for the first time quark-gluon plasma (QGP) emission calculated at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the strong coupling with in-medium radiation calculated with hadronic many-body theory. Freeze-out and surviving primordial $\rho$ decays are also included. The calculations are compared with the high-precision dimuon spectra measured by the NA60 Collaboration, and with STAR preliminary measurements of dielectron spectra and elliptic flow. We obtain effective temperatures extracted from the transverse-mass spectra, and we calculate the elliptic flow of the different dilepton sources. Our results suggest that dilepton measurements in the low-mass and high $p_T$ region can provide insight into higher-order corrections to the QGP emission rate.

title: Gaia's promise to detect compact-object binaries II: Predictions for dormant neutron star binaries in DR4 and beyond
abstract: With the fourth data release (DR4) from Gaia imminent, we predict neutron star (NS) binaries with luminous companions (LCs) expected to be detectable in DR4 and the final data release (DR5). We create realistic synthetic populations of NS--LC binaries in the Milky Way using COSMIC, assuming (a) observationally motivated initial distributions of binary properties, (b) metallicity and location dependent star formation history of the MW adopted from the FIRE-2 galaxy m12i, and (c) all relevant binary interaction physics, with the rapid and delayed supernova prescriptions. We estimate the detectable NS--LC population using an approximate Gaia\ selection function based on projected orbital size of the LC as well as gaiamock, which emulates Gaia's multi-epoch astrometry and orbit-fitting pipeline- both after taking into account extinction and reddening. Across supernova models and statistical fluctuations, the former (gaiamock) pipeline predicts $\sim14$--$29$ ($\sim1$--$8$), $4500$--$4700$ ($100$--$110$), and $4800$--$5000$ ($300$--$380$) detectable NS--LC binaries in DR3, DR4, and DR5, respectively. While the orbital-size based pipeline brackets the DR3 yield of NS--LC candidates, the gaiamock prediction falls short, suggesting uncertainties in the modeled binary evolution or contributions from other formation channels. DR4 is expected to directly shed light on the the relative importance of detectable NS--LC binaries from isolated binary evolution vis a vis other channels such as dynamical formation. Interestingly, our models suggest that future releases will also include $22^{+7}_{-5}\ (13^{+5}_{-4})$ and $124^{+14}_{-15}\ (53^{+10}_{-6})$ gaiamock-detectable pulsar--MS binaries in DR4 and DR5, respectively, for the rapid (delayed) model, which are prime targets for radio follow-up.

title: From the Early Slope to Curvature: Future Prospects and challenges for Astrophysical Parameter Estimation Using the Core-Collapse Supernova High-Frequency Feature
abstract: Gravitational-wave (GW) signals from core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) contain both stochastic and deterministic components. Among these, the High-Frequency Feature (HFF), associated with Proto-Neutron Star (PNS) oscillations, has emerged as an observable for probing dense-matter physics. Previous studies of the HFF have primarily focused on its early-time slope as a diagnostic of PNS contraction and its dependence on the nuclear equation of state (EOS). In this work, we investigate recovering higher-order features of the HFF evolution, such as its curvature, from core-collapse supernova numerical simulations. By analyzing 2D and 3D waveforms injected into real interferometric noise, we apply the coherent WaveBurst algorithm in its cWB-XP implementation to reconstruct the HFF of recovered events. Comparing reconstructions at different signal strengths allows us to examine the extent to which the HFF remains accessible beyond its early linear evolution

title: Evolution and afterglow emission of gamma-ray burst jets from binary neutron star mergers
abstract: Relativistic jets launched in binary neutron star (BNS) mergers are widely accepted as the engines powering most of the population of short gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Understanding their structure and dynamics-particularly during and after breakout from the merger ejecta-is crucial for interpreting GRB afterglows, especially for off-axis observers. Traditional models often assume simple angular or radial jet profiles, potentially missing key features emerging for jets piercing through realistic environments. This work aims to investigate the formation and evolution of the jet structure as it propagates through a non-homogeneous, anisotropic BNS merger environment. We focus on how the interaction with the ambient medium shapes the jet's angular and velocity distributions and assess the impact of this realistic structure on the resulting afterglow light curves. We perform a series of 3D relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of jets launched in post-merger environments, exploring different injection conditions. Simulations are evolved to late times, approaching the ballistic regime, where further dynamical evolution becomes negligible. From the resulting outflows, we extract energy and velocity profiles and compute multi-wavelength afterglow light curves using a semi-analytic model that includes radial stratification and the full 3D jet geometry. More energetic or earlier-launched jets drill more efficiently through the ejecta, but all develop asymmetries that leave clear imprints in the off-axis afterglow light curves. All models exhibit a complex multi-shock breakout structure responsible for an early, dimmer peak in the afterglow. Despite structural differences, all simulated jets are consistent with the observational data of the multi-messenger BNS merger event GW170817.

title: Early spectra of AT2017gfo from scaled 3D merger ejecta: mass--velocity distribution, 3D structure, and treatment of line opacity
abstract: We present ARTIS radiative transfer calculations for neutron star merger ejecta with line-by-line opacities, wavelength-calibrated lanthanide data, and time-dependent r-process compositions and thermalisation, testing how the early kilonova depends on the mass-velocity distribution, dimensionality, and line treatment. We rescale 3D dynamical ejecta from a merger simulation in density and velocity to approximate AT2017gfo. Mass scaling alone provides good agreement with the bolometric light curve but inconsistent spectra. With velocities additionally halved, the model also reproduces the observed spectra at 1.4, 2.4, and (albeit less accurately) 3.4 days. The Sr II triplet contributes most to the 10500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ peak, and La III and Gd III to the 13500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ shoulder. Although hydrodynamically not fully self-consistent, this model is to our knowledge the first kilonova model based on calibrated atomic data that reproduces the light curve and main spectral features of the early AT2017gfo, suggesting that total (dynamical plus post-merger) ejecta with higher mass, lower velocity, and similar composition compared to our dynamical ejecta could explain AT2017gfo. A 2D azimuthal average mixes lanthanide-poor with lanthanide-rich regions, smooths the density, and makes the averaged model three times fainter at 1 day and redder throughout than the 3D model, highlighting the importance of 3D modelling. We compare the line-by-line macroatom treatment with expansion-opacity and line-binned schemes with thermal redistribution, using identical atomic data. Luminosities agree to $\lesssim 10$ per cent after 1 day, but the expansion-opacity scheme, unlike converged line-binned schemes, overestimates the spectral flux by up to 20 per cent, which can bias inferred abundances.

title: Unpolarized Generalized Parton Distributions of the Nucleon in a Covariant Quark-Diquark Approach
abstract: We study the unpolarized generalized parton distributions (GPDs) of the nucleon in a covariant quark-diquark approach, in which both scalar and axial-vector diquarks are treated as composite subsystems. Motivated by previous form factor studies, we introduce a vertex correction based on the pion cloud picture as a first exploratory treatment of pion cloud effects at the GPD level, in order to improve the description of $E^q(\xi, x, t)$ and related magnetic observables. At the model input scale, only valence quarks are included. With the vertex correction, the electromagnetic form factors $G_{E, M}$ and the mass form factor $A$ obtained from the Mellin moments of the GPDs agree well with those obtained from direct calculations. The vertex correction brings the evolved charge weighted distribution $\sum{e^q E^q(\xi, x, t)}$ closer to the phenomenological parametrization. The correction shifts transverse strength from the central region toward the peripheral region, consistent with the long range character of the pion cloud contribution. The transverse structure results further suggest a harder longitudinal momentum distribution in the central region of the nucleon than in its periphery. Furthermore, the evolved real part of the proton Compton form factor, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}(\xi, t)$, has a reasonable magnitude and follows the main trend of the Quantum Deep Neural Networks (QDNN) extraction. In addition, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}$ may be more sensitive to the ERBL region than the other physical quantities calculated in this work.

title: Constraining Accretion Heating in Neutron Stars with Carbon Instability and Quiescent Cooling
abstract: In accreting neutron stars, different heating depths can produce similar quiescent cooling when the heating strength and core temperature are adjusted. For KS 1731-260, we compare thermal histories with accretion heating either in a shallower region that overlaps the carbon fuel layer or in a deeper region below it. Without the carbon instability condition, the two histories fit ten quiescent Chandra spectra nearly equally well. When local carbon instability is required at the observed superburst epoch, the deeper region needs stronger accretion heating than the shallower region. After the thermal and spectral parameters are refitted, the deeper history retains more heat beneath the fuel and produces excess early quiescent emission. A larger fitted absorbing column partly attenuates this excess but makes the late spectra too faint. The fuel temperatures at the superburst epoch are similar in the two histories, so the same prescribed energy release produces nearly identical superburst decays. Including carbon burial, consumption and nuclear heating reduces the accretion heating needed for rapid burning to begin near the observed superburst; shallower heating still fits the quiescent spectra better. This preference persists across the tested fuel depths, fusion rates, distances and absorption treatments. In synthetic examples, carbon in older material allows deeper heating to match the cooling of a shallower-heating reference. Inferring the heating location therefore requires a fuel distribution and thermal history consistent with ignition, burst emission and quiescent cooling.

title: Cold Magnetized Quark Matter under Compact-Star Conditions
abstract: We investigate the phase structure of cold magnetized two-flavor quark matter under compact-star conditions within a nonlocal chiral quark model with separable interactions. Electric charge neutrality and beta equilibrium are imposed in order to describe matter under realistic neutron-star conditions, while nonlocality is implemented through a Gaussian form factor. We find that low and moderate magnetic fields reduce the critical chemical potential for chiral symmetry restoration, signaling inverse magnetic catalysis. For stronger magnetic fields, the critical chemical potential becomes nearly independent of the magnetic field strength, Compared with the isospin-symmetric case, the combined effects of charge neutrality and beta equilibrium shift the first-order chiral transition to slightly higher chemical potentials, indicating that compact-star constraints delay the onset of chiral symmetry restoration. We further show that charge neutrality and beta equilibrium modify the de Haas--van Alphen oscillations in the quark density, shifting the Landau-level thresholds for the $u$ and $d$ quarks in opposite directions relative to the isospin-symmetric case. The effect on the chiral transition is small ($\sim 5$MeV) for fields $B\lesssim 10^{19}$G, relevant for magnetar interiors, and becomes sizable only for $B\gtrsim 3\times10^{19}$G. These results highlight the importance of incorporating realistic stellar conditions in studies of the QCD phase diagram at high baryon density.

title: Electronic-structure control of nuclear excitation by electron capture in finite-density 229 Th
abstract: Nuclear excitation by electron capture (NEEC) provides a unique pathway for coupling electronic and nuclear dynamics, but its description in dense matter commonly relies on electronic structures of isolated ions. Here we show how dense environments reshape the available NEEC capture channels. Using a finite-temperature average-atom model, we assess channel availability by jointly considering electronic localization, resonance energy matching, and vacancy availability. Near solid density, the shallow $6p$ states remain sufficiently localized to support resonant electron capture that drives the 8.356-eV isomeric transition in $^{229}$Th, whereas higher valence-like states merge into the continuum and no longer constitute localized capture channels. Calculations at different temperatures and densities reveal distinct windows of channel availability arising from the interplay among pressure-induced delocalization, shifts in resonance energy, and vacancy formation. Coupling the reconstructed channels to particle-in-cell simulations of laser-driven $^{229}$Th further shows that electronic structure at finite density can substantially alter the predicted cumulative NEEC yield. These results demonstrate how the electronic environment governs resonant capture pathways, highlighting its essential role in nuclear excitation driven by electrons in dense matter.

title: Observation of Strong Directed Flow for $\phi$ Mesons in the High Baryon Density Region at RHIC
abstract: We report measurements of the rapidity-odd directed flow ($v_{1}$) of $\phi$ mesons in 10--40\% Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{sNN}=3.0$--4.5 GeV from the STAR fixed-target program at RHIC, together with the collider-energy measurement at $\sqrt{sNN}=7.7$ GeV. Despite its mesonic nature, the $\phi$-meson $v_{1}$ exhibits a magnitude comparable to that of protons and $\Lambda$ baryons and is significantly larger than that of $K^{0}_{S}$ mesons in the high-baryon-density region. Comparisons with UrQMD calculations indicate that the observed $\phi$-meson directed flow is consistent with production through high-mass baryon resonances and the collective motion of baryons influenced by baryonic mean-field interactions. These results provide new experimental constraints on baryon-resonance production and strange-hadron transport dynamics in dense QCD matter.

title: Exact flavor conservation at the quark level in causal clusters: Strange particles, protons, and light nuclei in small collision systems
abstract: The suppression of strange hadrons in pp and p--Pb collisions at the LHC, including the $\phi$ meson, has recently been described by the exact conservation of strangeness imposed on the quarks of a causally connected cluster before hadronization. Here we extend this approach to the light flavors. The numbers of up and down quarks and antiquarks are conserved in the same cluster, and the suppression of a baryon or a nucleus depends only on how many light quarks of each flavor it contains. With the strangeness sector fixed by the previous analysis, a single constant, the ratio $r$ of light to strange quark abundances, determines the multiplicity dependence of protons, deuterons, He and hypertriton in pp and p--Pb collisions. Including the finite size of the nuclei, one obtains a very good fit of the data for $r=3.76\pm0.38$, i.e.\ strange quarks about 0.27 times as abundant as light quarks per flavor, close to the value known from string fragmentation

title: Beta-Particle Transport and Thermalization in Kilonova Ejecta with Detailed Atomic Microphysics
abstract: Abstract When two neutron stars collide, they eject material containing heavy nuclei formed by the rapid neutron capture process (r-process). As these nuclei decay, they power a bright optical/near-infrared transient known as a kilonova (KN). Modeling KN emission is a complex problem involving atomic opacities, radiation transport, and heating powered by the thermalization of radioactive decay products like γ-rays, α-particles, and β-particles. For heating by γ-rays, many KN modeling codes do full radiation transport calculations. However, heating by α- and β-particles relies on simplified descriptions of collisions and transport, and remains an important source of uncertainty in KN models. In this paper, we study the thermalization and transport of β-particles. To study thermalization, we use evaluated atomic physics data to estimate per-species contributions to energy deposition, scattering, and electron impact ionization, which we make available online. To include non-local effects, we develop a fully relativistic framework for charged particle transport in a spherically symmetric, homologously expanding ejecta, considering two limiting magnetic-field geometries. Non-local energy deposition and escape reduce thermalization efficiency, especially in the innermost and outermost ejecta, lowering the ejecta temperature and ionization state compared to local deposition models. Coulomb scattering partially offsets these effects by trapping particles at intermediate times ∼3 − 30 days post-merger. Ionization by secondary electrons significantly enhances the overall ionization rate. We provide analytic prescriptions for the spatially dependent thermalization efficiency for use in future light-curve calculations. Our results demonstrate that evaluated atomic data and charged-particle transport should be incorporated into the next generation of KN models.
source: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

title: α-decay properties of 216mTh and 217Th produced in 48Ca+Yb reactions
abstract: Abstract The α-decay properties of short-lived 216mTh and 217Th isotopes, produced in 48Ca+Yb fusion-evaporation reactions, were re-estimated using detailed analyses of the previously obtained data [R. N. Sagaidak et al. Phys. Rev. C 110, 044609 (2024)]. Recoil-α correlations extracted from the collected data were analyzed. Half-lives, α-decay energies, and their relative intensities wereconsistent with tabulated data for the isotopes under consideration. High production yields of observed nuclei provided more accurate estimates of their half-life values compared to previous studies.

title: Systematic study of pre-scission neutron and α -particle emissions in heavy-ion-induced fission reactions
Proton and neutron elastic scattering at low energies on He targets from \textit{ab initio} optical potentials
abstract: We construct and discuss $\textit{ab initio}$ nucleon-nucleus optical potentials at low energies for $^{3,4,6}$He targets. In this work, we use the $\textit{ab initio}$ SA-NCSM/GF approach that combines the $\textit{ab initio}$ symmetry-adapted no-core shell model with the Green's function technique to construct optical potentials, and extend this formulation to proton scattering and targets with nonzero spin. We show that these optical potentials reproduce experimental differential cross sections and phase shifts for proton and neutron elastic scattering remarkably well. The $\textit{ab initio}$ SA-NCSM/GF approach provides nonlocal, energy dependent and dispersive optical potentials, suitable for the astrophysically relevant regime of low energies and for exotic nuclei, where experiments are difficult and data is often unavailable.

title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
abstract: Abstract One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1–3 ). Achieving p -wave superconductivity 4 and its magnetic analogue 5 —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge 6,7 . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p -wave magnets 5,7–10 , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves S y polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted S y exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics 10 , topological matter 7 , superconductivity 11 and beyond.
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

title: Electromagnetic form factors of the hidden-charm pentaquarks in a coupled-channel unitary approach
abstract: We study the electromagnetic form factors of the hidden-charm pentaquarks $P_c(4312)$, $P_c(4440)$ and $P_c(4457)$ and of their four heavy-quark spin partners, treated as $\bar D^{(*)}\Sigma_c^{(*)}$ hadronic molecules. The states are poles of a coupled-channel unitary amplitude with a vector-meson exchange kernel that respects heavy-quark spin symmetry. The form factors are the residues at the double pole of the photon-coupled amplitude. The current consists of one-body currents and a photon--four-hadron vertex, which we construct for this channel space. Its gauged-kernel part ensures the charge normalization through the compositeness sum rule, while its contact parts contain couplings that the model does not determine. For $J^P=\tfrac12^-$, $\tfrac12^-$, $\tfrac32^-$ and pointlike constituents, the mean squared distances between the constituents of the three observed states are $0.85-0.47i$, $0.35-0.18i$ and $1.76-0.57i\,\mathrm{fm}^2$. Within $2\%$, they equal the zero-range value $1/(4\mu_{\rm red} B_c)$, with reduced mass $\mu_{\rm red}$ and complex binding energy $B_c$, times the effective-range factor of the amplitude. The real parts of the magnetic moments are $1.7$, $-0.9$ and $1.3\,\mu_N$, within $11\%$ of the additive moments of the constituents. Variations of the constituent moments and of the magnetic contact couplings within bounds from dimensional analysis give the ranges $0.8$ to $2.0$, $-1.3$ to $-0.2$ and $0.2$ to $1.8\,\mu_N$. The charge radii depend also on the constituent structure and on electric contact currents. The photon loops of open channels have a triangle singularity at spacelike momentum transfer. We specify the analytic continuation of the residue in $Q^2$ and give the difference between its two adjacent branches in closed form.

title: Transverse Energy--Energy Correlators at Small $x$ for Photon--Hadron Production
abstract: We study the transverse energy--energy correlator (TEEC) observable in photon--hadron and photon--jet production in p+p and p+A collisions at small $x$. We derive the relevant expressions in the high-energy limit of the scattering where the dipole picture is applicable and show how the dependence on the fragmentation function of the hadron cancels due to the momentum-sum rule. The nonperturbative scattering with the target nucleus is expressed in terms of the dipole amplitude, which also describes nonlinear gluon saturation effects. The TEEC observable is computed in the RHIC and LHC kinematics, and we show that it can be sensitive to the dipole amplitude, making it a potentially good observable for studying saturation effects.

title: One-point energy correlator for deep inelastic scattering at small $x$
abstract: We derive the expressions for the one-point energy correlator (OPEC) in deep inelastic scattering in the high-energy (small-$x$) limit within the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework. The OPEC is computed as a function of the angle between the energy flow and the target proton or nucleus, enabling a systematic exploration of different momentum scales in the scattering process. Owing to the momentum sum rule, the dependence on fragmentation functions cancels, leaving the dipole amplitude as the only nonperturbative input. As a result, the OPEC provides a sensitive and promising probe of gluon saturation dynamics at small $x$. We present numerical results for representative kinematic configurations relevant to the future Electron--Ion Collider, demonstrating sizable nuclear suppression effects within the CGC framework and highlighting the consistency of this observable with predictions from gluon saturation.

versions.abstract: We derive the expressions for the one-point energy correlator (OPEC) in deep inelastic scattering in the high-energy (small-$x$) limit within the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework. title: Inclusive and multiplicity-dependent pseudorapidity densities of charged particles in pp collisions at $\mathbf{\sqrt{s} = 13.6}$ TeV
abstract: The distribution of the pseudorapidity density of primary charged particles (${\rm d}N_{\rm ch}/ {\rm d}\eta$) in $|\eta|<1.5$ is measured in pp collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13.6 TeV using the ALICE detector. Tracks are reconstructed with the upgraded Inner Tracking System and Time Projection Chamber, and results are reported for events having at least one charged particle in $|\eta|<1$. The multiplicity dependence of the pseudorapidity density of charged particles is also explored with the multiplicity determined by the forward detectors. The average charged-particle pseudorapidity density at midrapidity ($|\eta|<0.5$) is measured to be $\langle \mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{ch}}/\mathrm{d}\eta \rangle = 7.10 \pm 0.20$. Combined with lower-energy measurements, the results follow a power-law scaling with the center-of-mass energy. These measurements provide a new reference for charged-particle production at the highest proton$-$proton collision energy available at the LHC.

title: Mean-field theory of superfluid-superconducting vortex states in the outer core of neutron stars
Astrophysical constraints on hadron-quark crossover in hybrid neutron stars
abstract: We investigate astrophysical constraints on hybrid neutron-star equations of state constructed by combining an extended linear sigma model description of quark matter with several representative hadronic equations of state through a smooth hadron--quark crossover. Four different hadronic models are examined in order to explore the model dependence of the resulting hybrid equations of state. After imposing stability, causality, perturbative QCD matching, tidal deformability, and maximum-mass constraints, only the eLSM+GMSR(BSK16) construction remains fully consistent with current astrophysical observations. The surviving parameterizations are further constrained using Bayesian inference based on NICER mass--radius measurements and the GW170817 gravitational-wave event. The posterior distributions favor a broad hadron--quark crossover occurring at relatively high baryon densities, while the formation of extended pure quark cores is strongly disfavored. Instead, the current observations favor neutron stars containing an extended mixed hadron--quark transition region. We also investigate the implications of the inferred maximum-mass distribution for the secondary object of GW190814 and find that, within the present model and adopted observational constraints, its interpretation as a neutron star is unlikely.

title: Recent achievements at the ITER Neutral Beam Test Facility, and mission within the ITER research plan
abstract: Abstract The Heating and Current Drive Neutral Beam Injectors in ITER will be essential in the DT phase to reach burning plasma condition and control advanced scenarios, providing at least 33 MW of heating power by neutral beams of hydrogen (0.87 MeV) or deuterium (1 MeV).The operation of a full-scale negative ion source (SPIDER) and a complete injector prototype(MITICA) are being validated at the Neutral Beam Test Facility (NBTF) in Padova, Italy,within a long-term strategy integrated with the revised ITER Research Plan. Following itsfirst major shutdown, SPIDER completed a validation campaign (SO-2), operating 320beamlets simultaneously for the first time, reaching ⁓700 kW beam power and an extractedcurrent density of 215 A/m2 in hydrogen at 0.3 Pa and RF power of 72 kW/driver – in linewith the scaling towards ITER target – together with a substantial increase in pulse duration.Meanwhile, MITICA completed a dedicated campaign on high voltage insulation in vacuum,demonstrating equivalent voltage holding up to 910 kV at HNB-relevant pressure using anintermediate electrostatic shield, a result directly relevant to the 870 kV target. Therestoration and improvement process of the MITICA power supply, damaged during the firstintegrated tests, is in its final phase ahead of the repetition of the full integrated tests.

title: Power corrections to heavy-quark spin correlations in small-$x$ deep-inelastic scattering
abstract: Heavy-quark spin correlations in small-$x$ deep-inelastic scattering receive corrections beyond the back-to-back limit. For a rotationally symmetric target at leading power, the target dependence cancels from the normalized spin density matrix after full azimuthal averaging, for fixed kinematics and spin axes related by transverse light-front boosts. We calculate the first nonvanishing correction at tree level for finite quark mass and finite $N_c$ in a homogeneous Gaussian target. The expansion through fourth order in the dipole sizes includes logarithms, contact terms and all interference contributions at that order. Comparison with the improved transverse-momentum-dependent approximation separates kinematic corrections from terms with additional insertions of the target current. Numerical integration of the unexpanded Gaussian kernel tests the approximation at 28 parameter points. Spin correlations differ between the two targets in all 12 kinematic comparisons; in one comparison both spin states remain separable. At fixed photon virtuality, the leading large-$P$ behavior of the fourth-order correction to the normalized transverse spin state is generically proportional to $m\ln P/P^3$. We also compare two fixed Gaussian targets using unpolarized momentum distributions and joint spin measurements. For a purely transverse photon, three narrow momentum bins and an ideal measurement of both spins along the common quark-momentum axis defined by the light-front boost, spin information adds 3.5-3.7 percent to the expected log likelihood ratio after the overall normalization is fitted. This increase depends on the spin analyzing power and bin selection. The results quantify a model-dependent effect under idealized measurement conditions.

title: Strangeness-to-entropy ratio across the QCD crossover
abstract: We study the absolute open-strangeness density $n_{|S|}$ of strongly interacting matter at vanishing conserved-charge chemical potentials. Unlike the net-strangeness susceptibility $\chi_2^S$, this quantity is not a derivative of the QCD partition function and requires a microscopic specification of the strangeness carriers. We use an equation of state that interpolates between an interacting hadron resonance gas and a quark-gluon plasma, with parameters fixed previously by lattice-QCD bulk thermodynamics. The ratio of $n_{|S|}$ to the entropy density $s$ follows the hadron-gas behavior below $T\simeq120$ MeV, rises above the ideal massless $2+1$-flavor limit of approximately $0.053$ across the crossover, and approaches this limit from above at high temperature. The same equation of state, minimally extended to finite $\mu_S$, captures the temperature dependence of the lattice-QCD $\chi_2^S$. For uncorrelated singly-strange Boltzmann particles, the strangeness fluctuation factor $F_S=\chi_2^S/(n_{|S|}/T^3)$ equals unity. Within the constructed equation of state, it deviates from unity by less than $10\%$. This allows us to estimate $n_{|S|}/s$ from lattice-QCD data on $\chi_2^S$ and $s$. The lattice-based estimate reaches a maximum of $n_{|S|}/s\simeq0.063$ at $T\simeq220$ MeV, followed by a $20\%$ decrease towards the high-temperature limit.

title: Precision Muon Physics
abstract: The muon has become a versatile tool for fundamental physics. Measurements of muon decay determine the Fermi constant and establish the chiral structure of weak interactions. Measurements with stored muons and bound muons enable precision determinations of the muon charge, mass, and magnetic moment. These studies also provide far-reaching tests of bound-state QED and the Standard Model, as well as unique sensitivity to physics beyond our current understanding of the particles, forces, and laws of nature. We survey the landscape of precision muon physics, emphasizing both the physics reach and the experimental breadth. We highlight the range of techniques, from charged-particle timing, tracking, and polarimetry to storage-ring experiments, microwave resonance methods, and Doppler-free laser spectroscopy. We also describe the interplay between experimental work and theoretical developments in quantum electrodynamics, quantum chromodynamics, and effective field theory.
