title: Efficient Iterative Symmetrization algorithm for quantum computing and hadron applications
abstract: Efficient algorithms for the (anti)symmetrization of quantum registers are necessary for upcoming few- and many-body physics applications, from atomic to particle-physics scales. We propose a recursive algorithm (anti)symmetrizing the last particle added to memory, each time one is created or destroyed, respect to the rest of already (anti)symmetrized ones. Given a generalized Dicke state (GDS) of $(j-1)$ quantum registers, each assigned to a particle, the algorithm produces another GDS of $j$ registers (of $n_{qb}$ qubits each) using a mere $\mathcal{O}(j\log_2^2 j + j n_{qb})$ $\mathtt{CNOT}$ and single-qubit gates, and $3j+\lceil\log_2j\rceil+\mathcal{O}(\max(n_{qb},\log_2 j))$ clean auxiliary qubits. The (anti)symmetrizing operator constructed for this purpose depends on the quantum numbers of the additional particle being introduced or ``created''. The algorithm improves upon the construction presented in Appendix A of \cite{Galvez-Viruet:2024hry} by almost two powers of $j$ and is on par with the most efficient methods to date, while ideally suited for dynamical memory management with variable particle number. We exemplify its applicability with a small selection of problems from hadron physics which are expected to be addressable with upcoming quantum computers.

title: Astrophysical Constraints for Bosonic Dark Matter in and Around Quark Stars
abstract: We investigate the structure, stability, and mass-radius relations of compact stars composed of quark matter within the non-ideal MIT Bag Model mixed with self-interacting bosonic dark matter with a $\phi^n$ self-interaction potential. By solving the coupled two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for boson masses between 200 MeV and 1 GeV and self-interaction strengths with $n=4$ and $n=40$, we show that strong self-interactions and higher boson masses enhance the stability of compact star configurations at high central pressures, though they reduce maximum overall masses. Ultra-compact solutions with $C \ge 1/3$ capable of mimicking black holes are significantly restricted compared to hadronic models, emerging only for strong self-interactions and dark matter fractions exceeding 90\%. Depending on the parameters, the compact stars form either extended dark matter halos or compact cores: stronger self-interactions and higher boson masses suppress the radial extension to favor compact cores of dark matter. Matching our models against observational constraints highlights PSR J1614$-$2230 and XTE J1814$-$338 as potential window of opportunity for dark matter detection. Notably, XTE J1814$-$338 could confirm a dark sector, given its requirement for light boson masses ($m_b \approx 200\text{--}300\text{ MeV}$) and strongly DM-dominated configurations.

title: Systematic investigation of Fission timescale and Fission time distributions using a Langevin dynamical model
abstract: Fission time scale and associated Fission Time Distributions (FTDs) provide important information on the dynamical evolution of nuclear fission and the competition between particle evaporation and fission. In this work, a one-dimensional Langevin dynamical model is employed to investigate the fission time scale and corresponding FTDs of the representative compound nuclei [Formula: see text], [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text]. The resulting FTDs exhibit distinct characteristics in the shapes and widths of the distributions, characterized by extended long-time components that significantly impact the average fission time. Further, to understand the transitional behavior, [Formula: see text] is studied in detail over a wide range of excitation energies. The excitation-energy dependence of the FTD and the relationship between the average fission time and the last-neutron evaporation time are analyzed to investigate the competition between neutron evaporation and fission. The results provide insight into the excitation-energy dependence of fission-time distributions and the competition between neutron evaporation and fission within the one-dimensional Langevin framework.

title: Characterization of the angular distribution of hot electrons generated in direct-drive inertial confinement fusion implosions
A Multimission Detection Framework for High-energy Transients: Application to a 13 yr Fermi/GBM and Swift/BAT Sample
abstract: Abstract The detection of faint high-energy transients is becoming increasingly important in time-domain and multimessenger astronomy, particularly for identifying electromagnetic counterparts to binary neutron star mergers, high-energy neutrino events, and other weak transient phenomena. At present, the sensitivity of gamma-ray and hard X-ray searches is often limited by the detection threshold of individual instruments, leaving a population of faint transients inaccessible to single-mission analyses. To address this limitation, we develop a joint detection framework that combines trigger information from multiple detectors and assigns each candidate a joint association probability, p joint , as a function of the individual detector signal-to-noise ratios. We apply this framework to archival Fermi/GBM and Swift/BAT rates data from 2013 to 2025. The method effectively separates coincident signals from accidental background associations, suppressing inconsistent coincidences while enhancing the significance of faint events observed by both instruments. We find that, under optimal conditions, a two-mission search can increase the accessible volume for short gamma-ray bursts by up to 60%. This framework provides a practical foundation for generalized multimission searches, enabling more sensitive exploration of the faint high-energy transient sky and improving the prospects for future multimessenger discoveries.

title: Universal Mass Equation for Equal-Quantum Excited-States Sets~III
abstract: Using our simple logarithmic Universal Mass Equation, we considered heavy non-$q\bar{q}$ meson states. PDG2026 reported a series of mesons with quantum numbers not allowed for standard $q\bar{q}$ states. Using LQCD predictions, we evaluated a scalar $0^{++}$ and tensor $2^{++}$ glueball series for which predictions are available. This approach allows us to predict heavy states that require future experimental studies. Additionally, we consider the possible misidentification of some meson states.

title: Probing jet-medium interactions in heavy-ion collisions using energy-energy correlators
abstract: Energy-energy correlators (EECs) provide a sensitive probe of both perturbative and nonperturbative dynamics in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Jet-medium interactions enhance particle multiplicity within the jet cone, which must be properly accounted for when extracting the EEC of jet shower hadrons in experiments. To address this issue, we develop an augmentation method that exploits momentum conservation between the near-side and away-side regions, using $\gamma$-jet events with 0-10\% centrality in Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV simulated with the CoLBT-hydro model. This approach yields an experimentally reconstructed EEC that shows improved agreement with the EEC of hadrons originating primarily from jet parton splittings. Comparing EECs of jets from Pb+Pb and p+p collisions with different matching conditions can be sensitive to jet medium interaction dynamics, and provide a novel means to test the scenario of jet energy loss in the QGP, followed by fragmentations outside the QGP.

title: Particle seismology: mechanical and gravitational properties from parton-hadron duality
abstract: The internal structure of hadrons is characterized by form factors which correspond to matrix elements of currents. Among those, the stress-energy-momentum tensor is a universally conserved quantity providing the gravitational form factors, from which mechanical properties may be derived via the response to the space-time fluctuations. They have received much attention because of their role as moments of the Generalized Parton Distributions, where the stress-energy-momentum tensor couples to two photons, and more recently, due to the explicit lattice QCD determination for the pion and nucleon. In these lectures we attempt a pedagogical review of the topic from a purely hadronic point of view, based on the notion of dispersion relations, meson dominance, and parton-hadron duality. We show that despite the overwhelming simplicity of the approach, a rather successful description of the lattice QCD data is achieved.

title: Open quantum system approach to the transverse momentum broadening of a colour dipole
abstract: Using the open quantum systems formalism, we study the propagation of a quark-antiquark pair propagating through a dense QCD plasma of size $L$ and transverse momentum broadening transport coefficient $\hat q$, and we derive the Lindblad evolution equation for the density matrix of the system. We focus on the boosted regime where the opening angle $\theta_{q\bar q}$ of this effective colour dipole satisfies $\theta_{q\bar q}\ll 1$. In the correlation limit where the quark-antiquark relative transverse momentum $p_\perp$ is much larger than the imbalance $q_\perp$ as well as the medium typical transverse momentum scale $Q_s=\sqrt{\hat q L}$, we demonstrate that the resulting Wigner distribution displays quasi factorisation between a hard factor describing the hard splitting producing the $q\bar q$ pair and the transverse momentum imbalance $q_\perp$-distribution encoding the broadening induced by the medium. The factorisation is violated by a "colour decoherence" factor that controls the $\theta_{q\bar q}$ dependence of the $q_\perp$-distribution through the ratio $\theta_{q\bar q}/\theta_c$, with $\theta_c \sim (\hat q L^3)^{-1/2}$. The open quantum systems approach enables us to clarify the role of this critical angle $\theta_c$ and its associated critical time $t_c$ in the genuine quantum decoherence of the density matrix in colour and kinematic space: in particular, $t_c$ controls both the suppression of the off-diagonal elements of the density matrix in colour space and the transition between singlet and octet states. We find, however, that colour decoherence sets in earlier than the full decoherence of the density matrix, thereby marking the onset of classical behaviour in the system. Finally, we investigate the corrections beyond the quasi-factorised picture due to the quantum diffusion term in $p_\perp$ of the Lindblad equation and we find that these corrections are mild.

title: Holographic Approaches to Hadron Structure
abstract: We give an introduction to and an overview of holographic approaches to QCD and hadron structure. After an introduction to the string-theoretic foundations of holographic QCD, we review the predictions of top-down and bottom-up models for the phenomenology of mesons, baryons, and glueballs. We focus on the top-down model following from probe flavor branes in the Witten model of low-energy Yang-Mills theory and, in the more phenomenological approach of bottom-up models, mostly on minimal models based on five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, which also implement global symmetries and their anomalies consistently, but allow the high-energy behavior to better match real QCD.

title: First Indication of Low-Energy Solar Neutrino-Electron Scattering with PandaX-4T Run 2 Data
Dispersive analysis of the $\boldsymbol{J/\psi \to \gamma \pi^0 \pi^0}$ process
abstract: We present a dispersive amplitude analysis of the low-energy $\pi^0\pi^0$ system in the radiative decay $J/\psi\to\gamma\pi^0\pi^0$, using the mass-independent BESIII $0^{++}$ and $2^{++}$ intensities, the total spectrum, and the measured $0^{++}-2^{++}$ $E1$ phase difference. The isoscalar $S$-wave is described by a coupled-channel $\pi\pi/K\bar K$ Muskhelishvili-Omn\`es representation, which implements the strong final-state interactions associated with the $f_0(500)$ and $f_0(980)$. The $D$-wave is treated with a single-channel $\pi\pi$ Muskhelishvili-Omn\`es representation, where we identify all kinematic constraints of helicity amplitudes before transforming them to the experimental $E1$, $M2$, and $E3$ multipoles. Smooth short-distance production of a pseudoscalar-meson pair is encoded in subtraction polynomials, while left-hand-cut effects are estimated and found to be numerically subleading. We identify the negative solution of the BESIII $0^{++}-2^{++}$ $E1$ phase ambiguity, after using the modulo-$\pi$ freedom of production amplitudes, as the phase solution compatible with unitarity constraints, showing that the measured phase information can be accommodated with the Omn\`es phase motion without requiring large additional phases. By normalizing the BESIII intensities with the extracted branching fraction, we fix the absolute scale of the fitted amplitudes, making them suitable as input for future dispersive studies of two-pion contributions to gravitational form factors.

title: Cryogenic Mechanical Loss of GaAs/AlGaAs Crystalline Coatings
abstract: Optical coatings with minimal thermal noise are essential for high-precision, laser-based metrology experiments. Substrate-transferred crystalline GaAs/Al$_{0.92}$Ga$_{0.08}$As coatings have the lowest thermal noise for high-reflectivity mirror coatings with $\lambda =900$ nm -- 12 $\mu$m. Time-frequency stabilization experiments have demonstrated that GaAs/AlGaAs mirror coatings have a lower noise floor than amorphous mirror coatings. These mirrors are now being developed at sizes $\ge 300$ mm for gravitational-wave detectors. In order to understand the coating's fundamental loss mechanisms, which cause thermal noise, we have performed the first measurement of the mechanical loss at cryogenic temperatures using a cryogenic, multimodal, gentle nodal suspension system, which operates from 12 K to room temperature. This initial measurement used a silicon substrate whose asymmetry produced excess friction with the nodal support. Accounting for this friction and Akhiezer loss in the substrate and coating, the mechanical loss agrees well with the thermal noise observed in experiments using cryogenic fixed-cavities with GaAs/AlGaAs mirrors.

title: A Predictive Nuclear Effective Field Theory from Wilsonian Renormalization Group Principles I: Medium-mass nuclei and nuclear matter
abstract: The predictive power of nuclear effective field theory (EFT) from few- to many-body systems is substantially restricted by regulator dependence. Wilsonian momentum-shell renormalization group (RG) offers a natural framework for cutoff-independent predictions, but its many-body implementation requires regulating single-particle momentum modes, which breaks Galilean invariance. RG scaling analysis shows that this symmetry breaking is encoded in irrelevant operators whose effects can be included explicitly or absorbed into higher-body interactions. Guided by Wilsonian RG, we construct a regularization scheme for chiral EFT contact interactions and predict binding energies of nuclei up to $^{40}$Ca using interactions calibrated only to $A\leq3$ systems. The predicted energies vary at the percent level and agree with experiment for $300\leq\Lambda\leq450$~MeV. The same scheme reduces the overbinding of symmetric nuclear matter obtained with conventional relative-momentum regulators. Our results suggest that some model dependence observed in nonrelativistic many-body calculations originates from treating EFT vertices as static, Galilean-invariant potentials rather than as field operators regulated consistently across particle-number sectors.

title: The Dancing Bonfire: An Unusual Persistent X-Ray Source in M81 Exhibiting Recurrent Luminous Flares
abstract: Abstract Short-timescale X-ray variability provides a direct probe of unstable accretion onto compact objects, yet extragalactic X-ray binaries (XRBs) with recurrent flaring remain largely unexplored. Here, we present a detailed X-ray study of M81F4 (2CXO J095524.2+690957), a persistently luminous X-ray source toward M81 that exhibits recurrent short X-ray flares. Based on multimission X-ray observations spanning two decades, it is found that M81F4 remains persistently bright at L 0.5−8.0 keV ∼ 10 38 –10 39 erg s −1 , while producing flares lasting a few hundred seconds and reaching peak luminosities of a few 10 39 erg s −1 , with an observed mean (minimum) recurrence time of ∼0.5 day (∼6 ks). The stacked flare profile shows a rapid rise followed by a slower decay, but no significant hardness evolution. Spectral analysis reveals that both the flare and nonflare states are dominated by a hard power-law continuum, with marginal evidence of highly ionized Fe lines in the nonflare state spectrum. These properties disfavor classical Type I and Type II bursts and have no close analog among known XRBs. We favor a magnetized neutron star accreting from an intermediate-mass donor at a persistently high rate, with the flares arising from instabilities at the disk-magnetosphere boundary. If confirmed, M81F4 might represent a hidden population of XRBs in which sustained, magnetically regulated accretion can lead to brief episodes of super-Eddington emission.

We favor a magnetized neutron star accreting from an intermediate-mass donor at a persistently high rate, with the flares arising from instabilities at the disk-magnetosphere boundary. If confirmed, M81F4 might represent a hidden population of XRBs in which sustained, magnetically regulated accretion can lead to brief episodes of super-Eddington emission.

title: Residual Ellipticity Driven by Intense Magnetic Stress in the Hot Neutron Star Era
abstract: Abstract A neutron star with a nonaxisymmetric mass distribution continuously radiates gravitational waves. The amplitude depends on the magnitude of the deformation and is crucial for gravitational-wave astronomy. We studied an evolutionary effect on the magnetically induced ellipticity in the neutron star crust. A large deformation at the hot era before solidification is assumed to be produced magnetohydrodynamically, and its fate at later times is due to the decrease in the force associated with the decay and redistribution of the current. Instead of simulating the evolution of deformation with the magnetic field over a long timescale, we estimate the ellipticity that remains after the formation of the solid crust by comparing two equilibrium models before and after solidification. The relic ellipticity is ∼ 1 0 − 8 ( B 0 / 1 0 13 G ) 2 in magnitude for a dipole field strength B 0 at the surface. This value was primarily determined by the magnetic field at the later time, with a weak dependence on the initial large deformation. The memory of the presolidification state was retained, but was small because the elastic force contributed little to the equilibrium.

title: Radiation-source displacement measurement based on spatial resolution characteristics of active pixel sensors
abstract: This paper proposes a noncontact, highly sensitive detection method based on the characteristics of complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) sensors and a weighted centroid algorithm. This method extracts the signals in an image with high precision based on an in-depth study of the signal characteristics in response to $$\alpha$$ particles. In addition, a quantification model for the uniformity of the sensor region responses under a collimated structure was constructed, which validated the response uniformity of the CMOS sensor. Compared with traditional centroid localization methods, the proposed algorithm improved the positioning accuracy and stability by 43.04% and 48.89%, respectively. For static source localization, the error decreased from 0.072 mm to 0.018 mm and gradually converged as the accumulated frame count increased. For a continuously moving radiation source, the predicted path closely matched the actual path, and the prediction error for the displacement speed of the moving source was less than 5%. Under low-frame-count conditions, the response time was less than 1 s. This method provides an effective solution for the noncontact detection of sub-millimeter micro-deformations, significantly reducing the cost of surface contamination detectors for nuclear facilities and driving innovative applications of CMOS sensors and $${^{241} \text {Am}}$$ in industrial nondestructive testing and radiation monitoring.

title: Properties of neutron stars with hyperons within a generalized relativistic approach
abstract: In this work, we study the effects of $\Lambda$-hyperons on neutron star properties employing a generalized relativistic framework for the equation of state (EOS). Different choices for defining the hyperonic couplings with different levels of parametric freedom are discussed. In all models, the predicted NS maximum masses are reduced compared with the purely nucleonic composition as expected. In the case of relating hyperonic couplings via $SU(6)$-symmetry arguments to the nucleonic ones, we find that NS radii for intermediate mass stars are shifted to higher values compared with purely nucleonic stars, in agreement with the existing literature. However, allowing for more freedom for the hyperonic couplings, the effect is strongly reduced, and the distributions in the NS mass-radius plane of models with and without hyperons become very close. We have also investigated how different nucleonic density functionals influence the hyperon matter composition and neutron star properties.

title: Optical Follow-up of Two Spider Pulsar Candidates: An Irradiated Redback and a Possible Double Giant Impostor
abstract: Abstract Compact binary millisecond pulsars (nicknamed “spiders”) are a growing class of neutron stars: more than 100 systems are known in the Galactic field, including more than 30 candidates where pulsations have not been detected. Here we report the results of an optical follow-up of two spider pulsar candidates: 2FGL J0846.0+2820 (J0846, a huntsman candidate in an 8.1-day orbit) and 4FGL J0935.3+0901 (J0935, with a 2.4 hr orbital period and proposed as a spider of either the transitional, black widow or redback subclass). We also analyzed their multiwavelength properties (infrared, X-ray, and γ -ray bands), in order to assess their nature and current state. The optical orbital light curves of J0846 change from double-peaked in 2023 to single-peaked in 2024, but we argue that they are not consistent with either irradiation-driven or ellipsoidal orbital modulation. Its spectral energy distribution shows evidence for two blackbody-like components with similar temperatures ( T ) and radii ( R ), which dominate the optical ( T 2 ≃ 6000 K, R 2 ≃ 1.8 R ⊙ ) and infrared ( T 1 ≃ 3400 K, R 1 ≃ 5.2 R ⊙ ) bands. Based on this, we argue that J0846 is not a bona fide pulsar candidate and propose an alternative identification: a detached double red giant. In J0935, we find a light curve with one flux maximum around superior conjunction of the companion, where the colors and inferred temperature increase, suggesting prominent irradiation from the pulsar. We place constraints on its companion base temperature (4000–4600 K), which support one of the three classifications proposed for J0935: a redback spider in the pulsar state.

title: Four-Loop Nonsinglet Splitting Functions in QCD
abstract: The scale evolution of parton distributions is governed by splitting functions. We compute the four-loop splitting functions in perturbative QCD that control the evolution of quark nonsinglet distributions. We confirm previous partial results and obtain, for the first time, fully analytic expressions for all nonsinglet contributions at this order. These allow us to extract the analytic form of the four-loop virtual and rapidity anomalous dimensions entering logarithmic resummation. We provide precise numerical representations of the splitting functions suitable for parton evolution.

title: Exploring the Origin of Slow-rotating Pulsars: Emission from STARS Simulated White Dwarfs
abstract: Abstract An increasing number of slow-rotating pulsars and long-period transients have been observed in recent years. The periods of these sources can be significantly longer than typical pulsar sources, ranging from ∼100 to 1000 s, or even longer. The observed periods and period derivatives predict high magnetic fields, higher than the Schwinger field, when we consider conventional pulsar models of dipole-driven emission from neutron stars. Interestingly, the periods of these sources are consistent with the current observations of white dwarfs (WDs). We explore the possibility of magnetic WDs, simulated using the stellar evolution code STARS , as the origin of some of these unusual pulsar observations. We simulate WDs with enhanced magnetic fields due to accretion after their formation. We also briefly touch on the more exotic possibility of super-Chandrasekhar WDs as the origin for these sources. We find that expanding the parameter space to include the possibility of a WD origin provides an alternate and viable explanation for these unusual observations.

title: Exploring PSR J0901-4046 as an Ultraslowly Rotating Neutron Star versus a White Dwarf
abstract: Abstract The source PSR J0901-4046 shows a very long rotational period of ≈75.88 s. In fact, its long period suggests that it could be a white dwarf. We examine the properties of the source and compare the outcomes under the hypotheses of the source being a highly magnetized white dwarf (B-WD) and neutron star. We find that assuming it to be a B-WD with a surface field ∼10 10 G explains many properties, including its storage/rotational energy, in turn, explaining luminosity. On the contrary, the neutron-star-based idea, particularly if examined under the conventional spin down mechanism, requires an unusually high surface magnetic field ≳10 14 G, even exceeding 10 16 G, depending on the obliquity angle and emission mechanism. The source also sits very close to AR Sco, a white dwarf pulsar, in the period and period-derivative plane. We suggest that the source is a B-WD. Along with AR Sco, the source being a B-WD constrains the death line model. The B-WD hypothesis alleviates the necessity of an unusually high magnetic field hindering pair production for PSR J0901-4046 under the neutron star hypothesis. We argue that some rotation-powered pulsars with extreme properties may possibly be white dwarfs rather than neutron stars.

title: Emergence of collectivity in the 0 2 + band of 92 Zr
abstract: The $2^+_2 \rightarrow 0^+_2$ transition in $^{92}$Zr was observed for the first time in a high-statistics decay study of the 10-day isomer $^{92m}$Nb. Its $E2$ transition strength of 8.9(7) W.u. is enhanced by 40% relative to the ground state band, providing evidence for a collective structure built on the $0^+_2$ state which is analogous to the deformed shape-coexisting configuration in $^{94}$Zr.

title: 3D MHD Simulations of Rotating and Magnetized Core-collapse Supernovae with the GPU-Accelerated GAMER Code
abstract: Abstract We present 17 3D magnetohydrodynamic core-collapse supernova (CCSN) simulations of a 40 M ⊙ progenitor using the GPU-accelerated GAMER code. We systematically investigate the effects of rotation (Ω 0 = 0, 0.5, and 1.0 rad s −1 ), magnetic field strength ( B 0 = 0–3 × 10 11 G), and resolution on the postbounce evolution. Our highest-resolution models achieve a resolution of ∼250 m in the proto-neutron star (PNS) and gain region within 150 km. Magnetized models exhibit substantial magnetic-field amplification, reaching ≳10 16 G near the PNS, largely independent of the initial conditions. A persistent local maximum in the radial magnetic-field profile develops at ∼10–40 km, fed by inward advection of amplified flux from the gain region, and migrates inward as the PNS contracts. The PNS-averaged magnetic energy per unit mass undergoes a two-stage amplification before saturating around 10 16 erg g −1 : a magnetorotational instability-driven stage that proceeds faster in rapidly rotating models, followed by an even faster, advection-driven stage that is most prominent in nonrotating models. In exploding models, the magnetic-to-turbulent energy ratio in the gain region reaches ∼1%, suggesting magnetic feedback may modulate the explosion dynamics. For a Galactic CCSN at 10 kpc, the gravitational-wave emission exhibits oscillation and standing accretion shock instability features detectable by the current LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network. In rapidly rotating models, the PNS-oscillation frequency decreases with increasing magnetic-field strength, providing a potential multimessenger imprint of magnetic-field amplification.

title: The Future Circular Collider as a photon-photon collider
abstract: The CERN Future Circular Collider (FCC) offers a unique programme of photon-photon interactions in electron-positron, proton-proton, proton-lead, and lead-lead collisions, by exploiting the high-luminosity equivalent photon fluxes associated with the charged beams. Within the equivalent photon approximation, the electromagnetic fields of relativistic charged particles are described in terms of fluxes of quasireal photons. The complementary photon fluxes, energies, and virtualities available across the FCC operation modes provide access to a broad range of two-photon invariant masses and associated physics measurements. Physics opportunities open to study are highlighted, focusing on the exclusive production of C-even resonances, including the SM Higgs boson and searches for spin-0 axion-like (ALPs) and spin-2 graviton-like (GLPs) particles decaying back into photon pairs. These prospective studies demonstrate the potential to observe photon-fusion production of the Higgs boson for all colliding modes, as well as sensitivity to photon-coupled ALPs and GLPs with masses extending up to the kinematic reach of FCC-ee and into the multi-TeV range at FCC-hh collisions, with significant improvements over existing constraints.

title: Nuclear mass calculation based on anisotropic kernel ridge regression and $\alpha$-decay chain recursion
abstract: Many short-lived or rarely produced nuclei defy direct mass spectrometry, but their masses are constrained by the $\alpha$-decay energies connecting them through decay chains. We combine anisotropic kernel ridge regression (AKRR), an extended Garvey--Kelson relation (GK16), and $\alpha$-decay chain recursion: AKRR learns the residuals between experimental $\alpha$-decay energies and WS4 predictions, GK16 removes residual local fluctuations, and the corrected energies convert a measured anchor mass into the target mass by exact recursion---replacing absolute-mass extrapolation with interpolation of relative decay energies plus exact algebra. The only data-adjusted quantities are the three kernel hyperparameters, fixed by leave-one-out cross validation. For the 22 nuclei whose masses were measured only after AME2003, the $Q_\alpha$ RMSD falls from 169~keV (WS4) to 108~keV (AKRR) and 65~keV (AKRR+GK16), and the mass-excess RMSD reaches 86~keV, versus 348 and 211~keV for WS4 and AKRR. Mass excesses are further predicted for the 122 nuclei with measured $Q_\alpha$ but no directly measured masses.

title: Dispersive analysis of the $\boldsymbol{\phi \to \gamma \pi^0 \pi^0}$ process
abstract: We present an analysis of the radiative decay $\phi \to \gamma \pi^0 \pi^0$ in a dispersive framework, where the two-pion subsystem undergoes strong final-state interactions that cover the $f_0(500)$ and $f_0(980)$ regions. We employ a coupled-channel Muskhelishvili-Omn\`es framework that allows for a consistent treatment of two scalar resonances and crossed-channel singularities induced by the Born and vector-meson exchanges. We explicitly verify the equivalence between the modified and standard Muskhelishvili-Omn\`es representations for vector-meson pole contributions when the isoscalar Omn\`es matrix is chosen asymptotically bounded, and we adopt the standard representation in decay kinematics. This yields, for the first time, a parameter-free dispersive prediction for the kaon Born rescattering, which provides a dominant contribution. To obtain a good fit to the KLOE and SND data, we employ a once-subtracted coupled-channel dispersion relation with heavier left-hand cut contributions and two unknown subtraction constants. The results demonstrate the consistency among the data for $\pi\pi$ scattering, $\gamma\gamma$ fusion, and $\phi $ radiative decay, thereby validating the underlying dispersive formalism and the input used for the hadronic Omn\`es matrix and left-hand cuts.

title: A Predictive Nuclear Effective Field Theory from Wilsonian Renormalization Group Principles II: Hidden unitary transformations
abstract: A fundamental challenge in nuclear effective field theories (EFTs) is to demonstrate the equivalence of interactions built at different momentum cutoffs and calibrated to the same set of low-momentum observables. Focusing on contact terms, we explicitly construct the unitary transformation that connects these EFT Hamiltonians. By replacing the conventional \emph{relative}-momentum cutoff with a universal single-particle \emph{absolute}-momentum cutoff, we show that this transformation can be systematically implemented using the similarity renormalization group (SRG) technique. The key insight is that such a regularization scheme enables a manifest decoupling of the many-body Fock space, avoiding transitions of particles in intermediate states into high-momentum subspaces associated with conventional \emph{relative}-momentum regulators. The derivation closely parallels the momentum-shell integration formalism of the Wilsonian RG flow. Reformulating the path integral in terms of unitary transformations allows a more intuitive, energy-independent analysis of nonrelativistic many-body systems within the EFT framework. In particular, this framework ensures that effective interactions calibrated in few-body sectors remain unitarily equivalent when applied to many-body systems, a central requirement not yet fulfilled in nuclear many-body calculations. We also show that the breaking of Galilean invariance due to the \emph{absolute}-momentum regularization induces irrelevant operators controlled by the RG scaling behavior, without introducing further complications. We numerically demonstrate our theoretical analysis using a one-dimensional toy model of bosons. These results provide a useful tool for analyzing the RG evolution of nonrelativistic many-body systems.

title: Thermodynamics of a chemical-potential-dependent Polyakov–Nambu–Jona-Lasinio model
On the feasibility of model-based regulation of vertical instability growth rate using out-vessel coils in ARC-like scenarios
abstract: Abstract In this work, we propose a model-based feedback controller that regulates the vertical instability growth rate (γgr )of a high-elongation, double-null tokamak directly, using only out-vessel poloidal field (PF) coils. High elongationraises the achievable plasma current and fusion performance but makes the plasma vertically unstable, and in afusion power plant the in-vessel coils that present devices rely on for stabilization may be absent, leaving onlydistant out-vessel circuits. The controller couples a machine learning surrogate of non-rigid, profile agnostic verticalinstability metric to a constrained quadratic program: the surrogate supplies real-time γgr estimates and, viaautomatic differentiation, the actuator sensitivities, while the program allocates coil voltages to track a targetgrowth rate, maintain double-null divertor balance, and respect electromechanical limits. We tested this method onthe ARC V3A power plant design configuration across 24 closed-loop simulations spanning equilibrium variations,actuator degradations, and transient disturbances. We achieved full or marginal success in 83% of these cases(full in 50%, marginal in a further 33%) and lose control in the remaining 17%; the failures map the boundary ofout-vessel controllability (occurring at the highest growth rates) and under actuator limits. The controller doesnot regulate boundary shape explicitly: separatrix geometry follows indirectly from growth rate and flux balancecontrol and would require a separate shape control layer for sustained scenario evolution.

title: On the Structure of the Nuclear-Clock Isotope $^{229}$Th Beyond Quadratic Order
abstract: Precision measurements of the exceptionally low-energy nuclear transition of $^{229}$Th, offer an extraordinary sensitivity to a variety of new light fields. However, interpreting such measurements requires nuclear-structure information beyond what is currently constrained by spectroscopy. We develop a systematic description of the electric multipole interactions governing the hyperfine structure of ${}^{229}$Th, including the hexadecapole contribution, and perform a symmetry-based analysis of the resulting hyperfine splittings in crystalline environments. Hyperfine spectroscopy generally constrains combinations of nuclear moments and crystal-field gradients, leading to degeneracies when higher multipole interactions are allowed. We then combine experimental nuclear observables, particle-rotor relations, and a deformed-Fermi charge-density model to investigate the electromagnetic contribution to the nuclear clock's sensitivity to variations in the fine-structure constant. We find that higher-order nuclear deformation and state-dependent differences in the radial charge distribution of the clock states can substantially alter the predicted sensitivity, introducing large uncertainties that are not constrained by existing measurements. Our results highlight the importance of combining nuclear and solid-state theory with complementary measurements, including spectroscopy of higher-spin states, to constrain the nuclear structure and improve predictions of the clock's sensitivity to new physics. Our symmetry-based analysis also provides a framework for using hyperfine spectroscopy to investigate local defect symmetries in crystalline hosts.

Energy Partitioning in Dust-catalyzed H 2 and HD Formation Revealed by Molecular Simulations Considering Nuclear Quantum Effects
abstract: Abstract Molecular hydrogen formation on interstellar dust grains is a key surface process, but the partitioning of recombination energy between the substrate and the nascent molecule remains poorly understood. Here, we use ring-polymer molecular dynamics (RPMD) with a machine learning force field to investigate energy partitioning during H 2 and HD formation on graphene at T = 25 K, 50 K, and 100 K, focusing on the chemisorbed-H recombination pathway previously identified as the dominant low-temperature channel on bare graphitic surfaces when nuclear quantum effects are included. The desorbing molecule retains approximately 84%–87% of the effective released energy, with only weak variation across the three velocity-initialization temperatures under the present sampling protocol. Within the retained molecular energy, rovibrational motion dominates at 25 K, whereas center-of-mass translation becomes increasingly important at 100 K. H 2 and HD show similar total energy retention, with modest isotope-dependent differences in their internal partitioning. The effective joint rovibrational distributions show a modest positive association between vibrational and rotational excitation. Purely radiative cascade calculations in the optically thin, collision-free limit yield formation-pumping spectra at all three temperatures. From 25 to 100 K, the rovibrational fraction of the emitted energy decreases from approximately 43% to 28% for H 2 and from 41% to 28% for HD, while the strongest lines remain in similar wavelength regions. These results provide an energy-resolved microscopic picture of surface-mediated energy redistribution and formation pumping in H 2 /HD formation on graphene.

title: Quality Control for the LGAD sensors of the ATLAS High Granularity Timing Detector
abstract: The High Granularity Timing Detector (HGTD) currently in the production phase will mainly mitigate the pile-up effect in the ATLAS forward region and serve for bunch-by-bunch luminosity measurements in the high-luminosity (HL) phase of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The HGTD utilizes Low Gain Avalanche Detector (LGAD) technology, covering the pseudorapidity range between 2.4 and 4.0, and provides high-precision timing information to distinguish collisions occurring close in space but well-separated in time. A pre-production batch of 8-inch silicon wafers was fabricated and a systematic quality control test campaign was carried out. This paper describes the Quality Control (QC) required for full-size (15 $\times$ 15 array) sensors, including leakage-current and breakdown measurements performed on all sensors at the vendor sites, as well as more detailed electrical characterizations at the participating ATLAS-HGTD institutes. In addition, the electrical characterization of full-size sensors after irradiation is reported.

title: Prediction of the tungsten behavior in a high power high current JT-60SA H-mode plasma
abstract: Abstract In order to prepare for possible future operation of JT-60SA with tungsten plasma facing components, a H-mode scenario of JT-60SA at high power and high current is considered as reference in order to investigate the tungsten transport behaviour and assess the amount of electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) which is predicted to be required in order to avoid central accumulation of tungsten. The modelling is performed with the ASTRA transport code in combination with the TGLF-SAT2 quasi-linear turbulent transport model and with neoclassical transport of impurities computed by the drift-kinetic solver NEO and the FACIT model. The impact of argon as additional seeded impurity is also considered, not only in the core behavior but also on the possibility of achieving tungsten screening in the pedestal region. The main result is that these H-mode conditions in JT-60SA achieve a so far largely unexplored domain of parameters, in which a reactor-like very low collisionality is combined with high rotation levels. In contrast to the usual domain of operation of present medium size tokamaks, where tungsten neoclassical transport is in the plateau to Pfirsch-Schlüter regime, in the predicted JT-60SA conditions toroidal rotation has a beneficial effect in increasing the strength of the temperature screening, enabling operation without any strong central tungsten accumulation and, in the most unfavorable conditions of high tungsten concentration and low rotation, requiring only 2 MW of central ECRH power to avoid locally negative electron heat fluxes in the center. Within the limited predictive capabilities of the present modelling approach for pedestal parameters, a sufficiently large and realistic domain of parameters in terms of argon concentration and plasma rotation, as well as of relative density and temperature logarithmic gradients, can also be expected to lead to the dominance of tungsten temperature screening in the JT-60SA pedestal.

title: Neutron-Rich Disks, Nickel-Rich Ejecta: Can Direct-Horizon Collapsars Explain Early $r$-Process Enrichment?
abstract: Very massive stars above the pair-instability mass gap may collapse directly into black holes surrounded by massive disks. These "direct-horizon collapsars" accrete at $\dot{M} \gtrsim 10\,M_\odot\,{\rm s}^{-1}$ and have been proposed to eject a substantial amount of $r$-process material, powering "super-kilonovae". We present the first three-dimensional general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of direct-horizon collapsars with M1 neutrino transport, following a $\approx 150\,M_\odot$ helium core from collapse through the escape of magnetically driven outflows. Extreme accretion rates neutronize the disks to $Y_{\rm e} \approx 0.1$-$0.25$ and, at early times, allow them to satisfy the gravitational-instability and cooling criteria for fragmentation. However, the strong poloidal fields needed to eject the neutron-rich gas promptly also drain the disks and lift their electron degeneracy. The neutron-rich ejecta composition is set in a brief phase, such that the ejecta carry $\sim 0.1$-$0.3\,M_\odot$ of nuclei with $A \geq 69$, including $\lesssim 2\times10^{-4}\,M_\odot$ of lanthanides, alongside $\sim 1$-$4\,M_\odot$ of $^{56}$Ni. Assuming proportional retention and mixing of Eu and Fe, these yields imply $[{\rm Eu/Fe}]\approx-0.4$ to $+0.3$, and simple dilution estimates permit enrichment at $[{\rm Fe/H}]\lesssim-2.6$. Direct-horizon collapsars are therefore potential prompt contributors to iron and $r$-process enrichment at low metallicity. Their predicted Eu/Fe ratios fall below those of strongly $r$-process-enhanced stars, but uncertainties in the relative yields, particularly of iron, may close this gap. The ${}^{56}{\rm Ni}$-rich ejecta would power luminous supernovae with rise times of weeks, potentially accompanied by exceptionally powerful gamma-ray bursts, rather than lanthanide-rich super-kilonovae.

title: Muon Collider: Towards the Energy Frontier
abstract: A muon collider has emerged as a compelling candidate for the next energy-frontier particle accelerator, combining the discovery potential of multi-TeV lepton collisions with a footprint and power consumption far smaller than existing or proposed hadron and electron-positron colliders. Advances over the past two decades in high-power targets, muon production and capture, ionization cooling, rapid acceleration, high-field magnets, collider ring design, and machine-detector integration have transformed the concept from a long-term vision into a credible path toward a future flagship facility. This review summarizes the physics opportunities, the accelerator complex's design and status, the unique experimental environment, recent technical achievements, ongoing international R&D, and remaining steps toward realizing a high-energy muon collider by the middle of the century.

title: Dynamical constraints on the companion mass from pulsar timing and cyclotron line confirmation in the supergiant fast X-ray transient IGR J16418--4532
abstract: Supergiant fast X-ray transients (SFXTs) exhibit extreme X-ray variability on short timescales of minutes to hours. This is driven by accretion processes that are still poorly understood. IGR J16418--4532 is an intermediate SFXT in which X-ray pulsations have been detected and which has been proposed as a candidate cyclotron line source, making it a key system for probing neutron-star accretion physics and magnetic field properties in this class of sources. We constrain the projected semi-major axis of the SFXT IGR J16418--4532 through a timing analysis and confirm the presence of a cyclotron resonant scattering feature, thereby characterising the nature of the compact object in this system. We analysed a 148 ks long observation and several archival observations using epoch-folding techniques to search for pulsations while correcting the photon arrival times for a range of NuSTAR RXTE values. We performed phase-averaged spectroscopy using several different continuum models and assessed the significance of the cyclotron line feature. We detect coherent pulsations with P_ spin = 1208.67 ± 0.04 s and P_ spin = 1209.4178 ± 0.0084 s in and PCA light curves, respectively. The pulsations exhibit a clear dependence on the assumed projected semi-major axis and are detected with the highest significance for a_x NuSTAR RXTE i = 55.1 ± 3.5 lt-s ( ) and 51.3 ± 2.6 lt-s ( ). The light curves show several flares, and the pulse profiles are found to evolve over the course of the observation. Sliding-window pulse profiles reveal the pronounced effect of the orbital delay on the pulse arrival times in uncorrected data, which is fully removed post-orbital correction. Using the inferred orbital parameters, we constrained the mass and radius of the companion star to be in the range of ∼12--18 M_⊙ and ∼13--16 R_⊙, respectively. We report the first successful constraint on the binary mass function of an SFXT obtained by considering the orbital motion of the neutron star. Spectral analysis reveals a robust cyclotron absorption line at ∼50 keV, independent of the choice of the continuum, suggesting a magnetic field strength of ∼5 G. NuSTAR RXTE 10^ 12 The cyclotron line confirmation and dynamical constraints on the companion mass indicate that IGR J16418--4532 hosts a neutron star with a magnetic field of B ≈ 5 G accreting from a ∼12--18 M_⊙ companion. We demonstrate that optimising the pulse detection by correcting the photon arrival times with trial 10^ 12 values rather than modelling the pulse arrival time delays offers a route to obtain dynamical mass measurements in other SFXTs whose variable pulse profiles limit the scope of conventional timing techniques.

title: Behavior of kinetic instabilities in a dynamically forming resonant distribution
abstract: Abstract Instabilities driven by energetic particles are central to the physics of a burning plasma. The majority of kinetic simulations and reduced models assume that the unstable distribution is already fully established when energetic-particle-driven modes grow unstable. In realistic scenarios, however, energetic particles may accumulate in the resonance on an effective timescale comparable to the growth rate of the instability, meaning that the formation of the resonant distribution and the growth of the unstable mode must be treated concurrently. We study the behavior of these instabilities in the presence of such a dynamically forming distribution, evaluating two distinct metrics which measure how close a mode is to its linear stability threshold and how close a mode remains to its nonlinear stability threshold. It is found that saturation at large $\omega_b/\nu_\text{eff}$ (where $\omega_b$ is the bounce frequency of deeply trapped particles and $\nu_\text{eff}$ is the effective scattering rate at a resonance), normally associated with strongly driven excitation, can be achieved even if dynamically the mode remains at all times near its nonlinear stability threshold. We extend existing analytic models for near-marginal and far from marginal modes allowing for a time-dependent linear growth rate, deriving explicit expressions for the mode amplitude evolution. These formulas are shown to agree with nonlinear kinetic simulations. The discrepancies between the case of a dynamically forming distribution and the case of a fully formed distribution are shown to be particularly pronounced for energetic particle distributions which relax diffusively. We interpret these results in the context of realistic experimental parameters, and propose an experimentally measurable figure of merit for a mode's proximity to nonlinear threshold.

title: 3D modelling of runaway electron deconfinement by MHD instabilities in ITER mitigated disruptions: from avalanche to termination
abstract: Abstract The effect of MHD instabilities on runaway electron (RE) avalanche and termination in ITER mitigated disruptions is investigated using MHD simulations with the JOREK code. 3D simulations show that the MHD stability during the current quench (CQ) is highly sensitive to the density profile and the initial current profile after the thermal quench. The impurity and electron density distributions play a dominant role by influencing the temperature and current-density profiles during the CQ. In the most unstable simulation case with high edge density and sufficient edge cooling, magnetic field lines stay globally stochastic for more than 10 ms, substantially reducing the peak RE current to kA level in the baseline simulation. To assess uncertainty in the diffusion-based fluid RE transport model, the parallel diffusivity is reduced from 10 10 to 10 9 m 2 s -1 in a reference case, giving an upper-limit estimate of 0.57 MA for the peak RE current. Due to limited diagnostic data during disruptions, the link between the current profile and CQ MHD activity has not been tested on a present-day machine. In cases with a multi-MA-scale saturated RE current, RE termination is found to be a slow process induced by plasma vertical motion and edge stochasticity, rather than a rapid collapse driven by intense global MHD instabilities. Such slow termination converts a substantial fraction of the magnetic energy into RE kinetic energy, increasing potential damage to the first wall.

title: Improved Pion-Kaon Identification in Heavy-Ion Collisions with a Two-Dimensional Transformation
abstract: Accurate identification of charged pions and kaons is essential for precision measurements in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, but becomes increasingly challenging at intermediate and high transverse momentum because of the increasing overlap of the TPC and TOF particle identification responses. In this work, we quantitatively benchmark a two-dimensional shift-and-rotation PID procedure that combines the $n\sigma_{\pi}$ and mass-squared $(m^{2})$ information. The benchmark is performed using Au+Au collision events generated with the AMPT model, where the detector response is modeled using $p_{T}$-dependent PID parameters extracted from STAR data. Since the true particle identities and input yields are known in AMPT but are not used during the reconstruction, the procedure can be evaluated through a direct closure test that is not possible with experimental data alone. The two-dimensional procedure is compared with a reference one-dimensional method consisting of an $|n\sigma_{\pi}|<$ 3 preselection followed by a Gaussian fit to the $m^{2}$ distribution. While both methods perform well when pion and kaon PID responses are well separated, the two-dimensional procedure provides improved yield closure as the PID distributions increasingly overlap at high $p_{T}$. The reconstructed-to-input yield ratio remains within 2\% of unity up to $p_T =$ 3 GeV/$c$, whereas the reference one-dimensional procedure shows a larger deviation. Reaction-plane $v_{2}$ closure tests show that both the reference one-dimensional and two-dimensional PID procedures reproduce the AMPT input $v_{2}$ within the statistical uncertainties over the studied $p_{T}$ range. These results demonstrate that the two-dimensional procedure substantially improves the high-$p_{T}$ yield reconstruction without introducing a detectable bias in the extracted $v_{2}$ under the STAR-like detector response considered here.

title: Energy calibration of bulk events in the BULLKID detector
abstract: BULLKID is a cryogenic, solid-state detector designed for direct searches of particle Dark Matter candidates, with mass $\lesssim 1$ GeV/c$^2$, and coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering. It is based on an array of dice carved in 5 mm thick silicon crystal, sensed by phonon-mediated Kinetic Inductance Detectors. In previous works, the array was calibrated with bursts of optical photons, which are absorbed in the first hundreds nanometers of the dice and give rise to surface events. In this work, we present the reconstruction of bulk events through the 59.5 keV $\gamma$-ray generated by an $^{241}$Am source, which emulates more closely the interaction of Dark Matter and neutrinos. The peak resolution is $5\%~(\sigma)$ and its position is shifted by less than $10\%$ with respect to the optical calibration. We observe that the resolution is further improved by a factor $2$ combining the signal from neighboring dice. These results confirm the performance of the detector in view of the physics goals of the BULLKID-DM experiment for dark matter search.

title: Development of large-size permanent magnet phase shifters for HEPS
abstract: To fully utilize the straight section space and achieve higher brightness, two beamlines in the first phase of the High Energy Photon Source (HEPS) adopt a tandem layout of double cryogenic permanent magnet undulators (CPMU), with a phase shifter employed between the two CPMUs to match the optical phases. However, limited by the diameter of the vacuum bellows, the operating gap of the HEPS phase shifters is relatively large, resulting in oversized permanent magnets and imposing higher requirements on the structural design and assembly methods of the phase shifters. After magnet blocks were assembled, demagnetization of the permanent magnet material was observed; nevertheless, magnetic field tuning was successfully completed under these conditions. This paper presents a comprehensive introduction to the design, fabrication, and testing of the HEPS phase shifters.

title: Suppression of Grain Boundary Nitrogen Degradation by Boron in Superalloys
abstract: Superalloys enable the hottest sections of jet engines to operate at high temperatures, but environmentally assisted degradation limits their lifetime. In polycrystalline alloys, nitrogen penetrates beneath the protective surface oxides, to produce embrittling grain boundary nitrides. Boron is added in trace amounts to improve grain boundary strength, yet its role, if any, in oxidation-related degradation remains unclear. Here we show that boron segregates to an internal nitride--matrix interface in a Ni/Co-base $\gamma$/$\gamma^{\prime}$ strengthened superalloy. Both B-free and B-containing alloys develop stratified chromia/alumina scales at 800~$^{\circ}$C in \SI{100}{\hour}, but the B-free variant produces larger, deeper and more elongated Ti/Nb-rich subsurface grain boundary nitrides. Correlative 4D S/TEM and atom probe tomography identify the particle as a chemically complex B1 nitride and reveal interfacial boron segregation. This shows that trace alloying as an alloy strategy can control damaging internal reaction product precipitation and growth by core-shell segregation.

title: Sub-electron noise with a buried-channel DePFET: characterisation of novel DePFET concepts
abstract: Depleted P-channel Field Effect Transistor (DePFET) pixel sensors combine Fano-limited energy resolution with fast, low-noise readout and are used in instruments ranging from particle tracking to X-ray astronomy. In this work, two novel DePFET technologies that address the two factors of the signal-to-noise ratio through fundamental changes to the intrinsic design are characterised: a buried-channel design aimed at reducing the limiting low-frequency noise by weakening the coupling between the channel and Si/SiO$_2$ interface traps, and a super-$g_q$ design intended to increase the charge gain by reducing the effective internal-gate capacitance. Their noise and energy resolution were mapped across the transistor bias space, over a wide temperature range (100-260 K) and for integration times of 0.4-9 $\mu$s (readout times of 2-19.2 $\mu$s per row), and compared with standard DePFETs as developed for the NewAthena Wide Field Imager (WFI). All three variants reach their lowest noise at about 155 K. The buried-channel device achieves an excellent equivalent noise charge (ENC) of 0.96 e$^-$ (at most 0.83 e$^-$ after subtracting the readout-electronics noise), demonstrating sub-electron noise over a complete 64$\times$64 DePFET matrix in a single readout, alongside a power consumption reduction of more than 50%. The super-$g_q$ DePFET shows a 2.6-fold increase in charge gain (about 1100 pA/e$^-$) but exhibits higher total noise due to an excess noise contribution. The results highlight the potential of the novel DePFETs, with the buried-channel technology offering immediate benefits for low-noise applications such as the WFI.

title: Optimisation of importance sampling implementation in rare-event shielding simulations using Geant4
abstract: Rare-event search experiments demand ever-lower backgrounds, and the resulting radio-pure materials and suppressive shielding make related background simulations computationally expensive without event biasing. We present a method for optimising the widely used importance splitting and Russian roulette technique for rare-event searches, in which a whole number of equal-width importance layers fill the shielding geometry. Balancing relative uncertainty against execution time, we optimise the layer thickness for both $\gamma$-rays and neutrons, and across different shielding materials and thicknesses. Expressed as a multiple of the primary particle's mean free path, the optimal thickness generalises across energies for a given particle type and yields a physics-based prediction applicable to any shielding design. The same trend reveals that over-biasing is possible, with relative uncertainty worsening at high layer counts for fixed execution time. The optimal configuration gives an $\mathcal{O}$(20) gain in computational efficiency over the unbiased case.

title: Cancellation of cryocooler-induced vibration in trapped-ion systems
abstract: Mechanical cryocoolers offer numerous benefits for the operation of vacuum systems containing trapped atomic ions. However, the fidelity of laser-based gates can be degraded by phase noise induced by the cryocooler vibrations. We present a feed-forward vibration-cancellation system that directly measures inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer and applies a compensating phase correction to the laser drive. The interferometer signal is demodulated, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) system unwraps the displacement measurement signal, computes the required correction phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator (AOM) to correct for the vibration-induced dephasing. With cancellation active, the qubit coherence time improves from $3.0\pm0.4$ ms to $35\pm5$ ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. We further validate the cancellation by artificially increasing the mechanical coupling of the cryocooler to the vacuum chamber. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by a factor of approximately 70 at an RMS (root mean square) displacement of 0.65 $\mathrm{\mu}$m.

title: A search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst in the M81 globular cluster, FRB 20200120E
abstract: Abstract We present a search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst FRB 20200120E, which is located in a globular cluster of M81 and is the closest known extragalactic FRB. We observed FRB 20200120E simultaneously with the high-speed, quintuple-beam optical camera HiPERCAM on the 10.4 m Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Effelsberg 100 m Radio Telescope. We detected one radio burst of fluence $\mathcal {F}_{\rm R} = 0.14\pm 0.01$ Jy ms during our observations, but found no evidence for corresponding optical bursts in the 11.98 ms frames. We find 5σ upper limits on the optical burst fluence of $\mathcal {F}_{\rm O} < 1.8\times 10^{-3}$ Jy ms (combined usgsrsiszs-bands) and the optical burst energy of EO < 5.4 × 1036 erg (rs-band), corrected for interstellar extinction. We compare our upper limit on the optical-to-radio fluence ratio $\mathcal {F}_{\rm O}/\mathcal {F}_{\rm R} < 0.013$ to various emission models involving inverse-Compton scattering in the magnetosphere or nebula of a highly-magnetised neutron star.
source: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

title: Proton generalized parton distributions from electromagnetic form factors: A theoretically constrained phenomenological reconstruction
abstract: We present a theoretically constrained phenomenological reconstruction of the unpolarized, chiral-even, leading-twist proton generalized parton distributions $H^q$ and $E^q$. At zero skewness, valence-quark distributions are combined with flavor-dependent exponential profiles calibrated simultaneously against phenomenological representations of the proton and neutron electromagnetic form factors. The construction imposes exact valence and anomalous-magnetic-moment normalizations, the low-scale condition $B^{u+d}(0)=0$, the required endpoint behavior, and the complete Gaussian impact-parameter positivity bound. The resulting parametrization provides a reasonable description of the electromagnetic form factors and their slopes while revealing the tension between strict GPD consistency and a precision reproduction of all low-$Q^2$ observables within the adopted ansatz. We extend the distributions to nonzero skewness using normalized double distributions and introduce an independent $D$-term to complete the relevant Mellin polynomials. We examine electromagnetic and energy--momentum-tensor form factors, impact-parameter distributions, positivity, polynomiality, and illustrative mechanical properties. The analysis distinguishes information constrained by electromagnetic data from additional assumptions governing skewness and the mechanical sector, thereby providing a transparent elastic baseline for future studies of nucleon-to-resonance transition GPDs.

title: Target-space fusion of classical topological defects
Antisymmetrization of composite fermionic states for quantum simulations of nuclear reactions in first-quantization mapping
Relativistic tidal excitation of g- and i-modes in neutron star binaries
abstract: When the gravitational wave frequency of an inspiraling binary matches a normal-mode frequency of a neutron star (NS), the mode can be resonantly excited. The excitation transfers orbital energy to the star and shifts the phase of the emitted gravitational-wave (GW) signal, thereby providing a potential probe of the NS interior. However, estimates of this phase shift in the literature vary by orders of magnitude due to different approximations and formulations used in calculating the tidal coupling strength. We revisit this problem using a fully relativistic scattering formalism, which serves as our benchmark calculation and provides a gauge-invariant mode response together with an effective tidal-mode coupling strength. We calculate the phase shifts induced by the excitation of stratification g-modes, crustal interface i-modes, and hadron-quark interface i-modes, and estimate their detectability with Fisher-matrix forecasts for current and next-generation detectors. In our models, direct g-mode excitation remains below the detection thresholds, even for the strongest stratification considered. Crust-core i-modes at large shear speeds provide the most favorable prospects and crust melting can produce a substantially larger phase shift. Hadron-quark i-modes remain below the next-generation detection thresholds.

title: Surrogate-assisted beam distribution shaping at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and Super Proton Synchrotron
abstract: The Super Proton Synchrotron at CERN delivers protons to the North Area experimental facility at 400 GeV/c. The extracted beam is split twice vertically in the transfer line with Lambertson septa to serve three fixed-target experiments simultaneously. A significant fraction of the beam is lost during these splitting processes, driving radioactive activation of the Lambertson septa. This contribution investigates reducing the splitting losses by optimising the vertical beam distribution before extraction. The developed method relies on resonant excitation with the transverse damper, reshaping the Gaussian vertical profile into a uniform and ultimately bimodal distribution, with the excitation amplitude acting as a single continuous control knob. A loss reduction of up to 23.5 % was measured. In simulations, the vertical amplitude detuning is established as a second knob that reduces the resulting beam envelope. This technique was verified with measurements at the CERN Proton Synchrotron. Surrogate models based on generative deep learning were developed for efficient real-time validation and Bayesian system identification.

title: LH$\mu$C Concept: Energy-Frontier Antimuon-Proton Collisions at CERN
abstract: The concept of the LH$\mu$C, an energy-frontier antimuon-proton collider based on the HL-LHC, is presented. After recalling why energy-frontier lepton-hadron colliders are indispensable as QCD explorers and reviewing the history of muon-proton collider proposals, two ways of realising $\mu p$ collisions at the LHC are compared: with muon-collider beams and with ultra-cold $\mu^+$ beams as proposed for $\mu$TRISTAN. For the latter, a $\mu$TRISTAN-type booster and the re-use of the LHeC energy-recovery-linac tunnel are discussed; colliding 1 TeV antimuons with 7 TeV protons gives $\sqrt{s}=5.3$ TeV and peak luminosities of $8.8\times10^{33}$ and $7.2\times10^{33}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, respectively. The detector concept and the physics potential, including searches for colour-octet muons and R-parity-violating squarks, are discussed together with the main challenges.

title: Effect of plasma beta on the access to marginal suppression of type-I ELMs with n = 4 resonant magnetic perturbations in EAST
abstract: Abstract We present experimental observations of marginal suppression of large Type-I Edge Localized Modes (ELMs) using $n = 4$ Resonant Magnetic Perturbations (RMPs) in the EAST tokamak, with energy confinement maintained.The edge safety factor and the normalized plasma beta are relevant to the ITER baseline scenario, $q_{95}\approx3.1$ and $\beta_N\approx1.8$--$2.0$.Marginal ELM suppression was observed when $\beta_N$ exceeded 1.8, with tungsten divertors and low recycling conditions.To investigate the underlying mechanism, quasi-linear modeling is performed, revealing that an increased plasma beta enhances the plasma response and the associated neoclassical toroidal viscosity (NTV) torque, reducing the RMP coil current required for field penetration.The findings suggest that increasing $\beta_N$ facilitates the transition from ELMy H-mode to marginal ELM suppression, which is favourable for ELM control with high-$n$ RMPs in future fusion devices, including ITER.

title: Control of the bootstrap current in approximately quasi-axisymmetric magnetic fields
abstract: Quasi-axisymmetric stellarators are the stellarator analog of axisymmetric tokamaks, retaining many of their favorable confinement properties, their compactness, and their relative coil simplicity, while avoiding their principal limitation, the need for an inductively driven plasma current. Despite these attractive physics properties, the development of quasi-axisymmetric configurations has been severely constrained by the absence of an experimentally validated divertor concept compatible with their large bootstrap current. In this article, approximately quasi-axisymmetric fields, complemented with piecewise omnigenous perturbations, are proposed as the basis for a strategy towards a stellarator reactor that potentially achieves, simultaneously, simple coil geometries, tokamak-like confinement, and, through tailoring of the bootstrap current, compatibility with an island divertor. Implications for attaining a high bootstrap current fraction in tokamak devices are also discussed.

title: Conformal Uncertainty Quantification of a Normalizing Flow Surrogate for the FACET-II Two-Bunch Beam
abstract: Fast surrogate models of the beam can be used for tuning, diagnostics, and control where end-to-end simulation is too slow. At FACET-II, a normalizing flow surrogate predicts the 6D high peak current two-bunch beam used for plasma wakefield acceleration (PWFA) in less than a second, from 37 injector and linac machine parameters (such as the RF phases controlling the bunch compression). However, a surrogate can predict an incorrect beam that seems plausible, so operators and controllers need to know when to trust its predictions. We use conformal prediction to generate a prediction-specific uncertainty with guaranteed coverage. That is, if we sample new machine parameters from the same distribution as our calibration data, the uncertainty will cover the simulation output at least 90% of the time. We provide two implementations: prediction intervals for beam parameters with fixed and adaptive widths, and a region in the full 6D phase space covering 95% of the electrons, 90% of the time. The median size of this region is 5 (drive) and 2 (witness) times smaller than a Gaussian ellipsoid with the same coverage. Across 1,000 independent test simulations, our prediction intervals identify failure cases for the surrogate, specifically the slice peak current of highly compressed bunches.

title: Advanced computational methodologies for water activation assessment and applications to JET
abstract: Abstract In water-cooled D-T fusion tokamaks, such as the Joint European Torus (JET), neutron activation of flowing water generates short-lived radionuclides ( 16 N, 17 N and 19 O), producing a distributed source of high-energy gamma radiation and delayed neutrons. The energy and intensity of the source are driving factors in the design of cooling and shielding systems and, if not understood early in the design, can lead to significantly increased costs. While several past and future experiments provide fusion-relevant water activation benchmarking data, the JET water circuit is the first to use a fusion tokamak environment. This provides a unique opportunity to benchmark fluid activation codes for applicability to ITER and other fusion devices, with a relevant deuterium-tritium (D-T) 14 MeV neutron spectrum, and a large water-cooling pipe network. The part of the network monitored includes the neutral beam injector (NBI) duct scraper and cooling for the rotary high vacuum valve (RHVV), which forms part of the same duct. Several computational tools have been developed in order to calculate the activation of moving fluids in fusion environments. These utilise a variety of approaches to couple neutron activation, fluid dynamics and radiation transport. The JET water circuit poses a challenge to tools which utilise computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to replicate the transport of water through a system. This manuscript details the analysis of the JET cooling circuit with the GammaFlow code and the comparison with experimental results. It is found that the code is able to reproduce the water travel time and detector pulse shape with reasonable accuracy. The activity concentration of 16 N is calculated with an average C/E=0.9 -0.3 +0.2 for the pulses evaluated. This is an important benchmark analysis demonstrating that fluid activation codes are capable of accurate predictions of radiation dose maps for future water-cooled fusion devices.

title: Relativistic Navier-Stokes description of the quark-gluon plasma radial flow
abstract: Using relativistic Navier-Stokes in the well-posed Bemfica-Disconzi-Noronha-Kovtun (BDNK) formulation, with a QCD equation of state and transport coefficients, we perform simulations that describe the radial flow in central Pb-Pb collisions measured at the LHC, providing a proof of principle for its viability in heavy-ion phenomenology. We identify causal frames that retain the Landau-frame interpretation, and verify frame robustness. M\"uller-Israel-Stewart simulations with identical input show large second-order effects, exceeding the frame dependence of relativistic Navier-Stokes, as well as causality violations.

title: Active Galactic Nuclei as Beyond the Standard Model Laboratories: a White Paper
abstract: Multi-messenger and multi-wavelength observations of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) can provide otherwise inaccessible knowledge about physics Beyond the Standard Model (BSM), and may even lead to its discovery. Realizing this potential hinges on two parallel efforts: advancing our understanding of AGN and of the dark matter around them, and identifying the BSM signatures that are at once promising and robust against the gaps in that understanding. These fields have attracted growing interest in recent years, also motivated by the IceCube association of neutrinos to individual AGN, yet we have only begun to explore their cross-fertilization. This white paper offers a new perspective on this interdisciplinary endeavor. It concisely reviews the state of the art in each field and at their interface, and identifies the key open questions that must be addressed to strengthen our prospects for learning about BSM physics with AGN.

title: Surface-muon production for ultraslow-muon sources of $\mu^+$-based colliders
abstract: Anti-muon colliders based on ultraslow muons, such as $\mu$TRISTAN and the $\mu^+p$ collider LH$\mu$C, need muon intensities well beyond those of present facilities. We study surface-\mup\ production by 3~GeV protons in graphite, molybdenum and tungsten targets with Geant4, for single, tilted and multi-layer target geometries. As single targets, molybdenum and tungsten give comparable yields, more than twice that of graphite, because a larger fraction of the beam interacts. Tilting a target with respect to a narrow beam and splitting it into several layers both raise the yield substantially: five-layer Mo and W targets give 6--8 times the surface-muon yield quoted for the J-PARC MLF graphite target, counted at the production target before capture and transport.

title: Polarised X-ray emission from the accreting millisecond pulsar SAX J1808.4-3658 during an X-ray outburst and a type-I X-ray burst
abstract: Modelling the X-ray pulse profiles of accreting millisecond pulsars (AMSPs) is a key technique for constraining the masses and radii of neutron stars. To this end, measuring the properties of polarised X-rays provides crucial information on the system geometry. We present the significant detection by IXPE of linearly polarised 2-8 keV X-rays during the decay of the 2025 outburst of the 2.5 ms AMSP SAX J1808.4-3658, with an average polarisation degree of $2.9\%\pm0.5\%$ and a polarisation angle of $46{\deg}\pm5{\deg}$ (measured East of celestial North), offset by $\sim 16{\deg}$-$24{\deg}$ from the average direction observed in the optical band over various epochs during the main part of the outburst. The observed degree of X-ray polarisation is similar to that found in the only other source of this class that has been targeted so far. By using a pulse-phase timing solution obtained with IXPE and NuSTAR, which confirms the long-term evolution of the pulsar spin and orbit, we did not find any significant pulse phase-resolved variability in the normalised Stokes parameters. Interpreting the polarised X-rays as originating from hot spots on the NS surface indicates they are almost aligned with the spin axis. We also report an indication for linearly polarised emission with a degree of $16\%\pm6\%$ (2-6 keV) during the peak of a type-I thermonuclear X-ray burst, with an angle almost orthogonal to that of the persistent emission. If confirmed, this level would exceed expectations for X-rays reflected by a thin accretion disc.
