title: Scalar charge of neutron stars and accreting black holes in Starobinsky gravity: quasi-universal relations, the trace anomaly and gravitational-wave sensitivity
abstract: The Starobinsky scalaron is sourced by the trace of the stress--energy, so its exterior charge is set by the matter around an object and not by the object's vacuum geometry. We derive a master formula for that charge for any static, spherically symmetric source, evaluate it first for neutron stars, where the interior is known, and then for accreting black holes, where it is not. For a star the pressure subtracts: on the interior metric with the Eardley sensitivity, and the charge is a quasi-universal function of the compactness. Six realistic equations of state confirm the relation but lie above the coefficient calibrated on polytropes; the refit reproduces their mean to 0.007. The trace $\rho-3p$ changes sign in the cores of massive stars, and the charge also tracks the tidal deformability and the moment of inertia to a few parts in 1000 and 100. Solving the Einstein-frame structure equations self-consistently moves a star along this relation and leaves its charge at fixed compactness within 4 per cent of the test-field value. We compare the charge with NICER radii and the GW170817 tidal deformability, and use the published massless dipole constraint from GW230529 to calibrate a Fisher estimate of the sensitivity of a similar binary to a finite scalaron range, projected to the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer; the range is a free parameter, and the laboratory bound on pure $R+\alpha R^2$ is confronted explicitly. A vacuum black hole has q=0; a hole with a disc has $q=\sinh(m_\phi r_d)/(m_\phi r_d)$, controlled by the disc's outer edge, which makes it the counterpart in which the same integral is dominated by matter far from the centre; light is blind to the charge at leading order, and the correction beyond it is negligible for any self-consistent disc.

title: Quark + diquark description of nucleon gravitational form factors
abstract: We present parameter-free predictions for the nucleon gravitational form factors (GFFs) using a Poincare-covariant quark+diquark Faddeev equation. We provide the full GFFs ($A$, $J$, $D$, and $\bar{c}$) along with their species decompositions into quark and gluon contributions. Based on the diquark breakdown, we find that while the scalar diquark component dominates the nucleon's energy, spin, and mechanical properties, the axial-vector component plays an indispensable role. The GFF $B(Q^2)$ is predicted to be vanishingly small but nonvanishing at finite $Q^2$; its physical origin is deeply rooted in the nucleon' s internal structure through cancellations in both the diquark content and the $u/d$ flavor sectors. Furthermore, our results for $\bar{c}(Q^2)$ confirm the fundamental symmetry requirements of the approach. Compared with lQCD, our calculated $D$-term and various spatial radii are somewhat smaller in magnitude. This systematic underestimation is primarily driven by the gluon sector and can be attributed to the omission of meson cloud effects, suggesting that these effects impact the gluon distribution more significantly than the quark distribution. Finally, our analysis of the energy density based on two extrapolation schemes reveals that the presence of a negative central energy density is highly model-dependent.

title: Magnetic Power in Binaries: From Coalescing Binary Neutron Stars to Close-in Exoplanetary Systems
abstract: A binary system containing two magnetic components ("stars") can be modeled as a circuit powered by the orbital motion, with the magnetic field lines linking the two stars serving as wires. When the total resistance in the binary components is small -- as found in many astrophysical systems such as binary neutron stars and extra-solar hot-Jupiter or super-Earth systems -- the connected field lines are twisted and open up in a quasi-cyclic manner, leading to quasi-periodic energy dissipation and flares. We derive analytic expressions for the average and episodic magnetic powers from such systems, providing a quantitative description on how the powers depend on the magnetic orientations of the two stars. The power can be much larger than in the case where one of the stars has a negligible magnetic field. It may manifest as pre-merger quasi-cyclic flares in coalescing neutron-star binaries and as orbit-regulated radio emissions in exoplanetary systems.

title: Shell structure and spontaneous decay of superheavy Z = 124 isotopes with the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum
abstract: Shell structure and spontaneous decay of $Z = 124$ isotopes are systematically investigated using the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum (DRHBc) with the PC-PK1 density functional. By accounting for deformation and continuum effects, the neutron drip line is predicted to be located at $N = 320$, and eight potential multi-neutron emitters beyond the neutron drip line are identified. The results, compared with the spherically constrained case, highlight the critical role of deformation effects in determining the ground-state properties of superheavy nuclei. In addition, potential neutron shell closures emerge at $N = 258$ and $350$, alongside subshell closures at $N = 232$ and $320$. The results disfavor $Z = 124$ as a possible proton magic number and suggest $Z = 120$ and $138$ as more favorable candidates for proton shell closures in the superheavy region. Finally, the competition between $\alpha$ decay, $\beta$ decay, and spontaneous fission is analyzed by calculating half-lives within various semi-empirical formulas. The results indicate that $\alpha$ decay is the predominant mode on the proton-rich side, whereas spontaneous fission and $\beta^-$ decay gradually become dominant with increasing neutron number.

title: Observation of $^{71}$Cr and expanded cross-section measurements and analysis of $^{82}$Se fragmentation
abstract: Production cross sections for neutron-rich nuclei from the fragmentation of $^{82}$Se were measured, including the previously unobserved isotope $^{71}$Cr. Particle identification of the mass number ($A$), atomic number ($Z$), and ionic charge state ($q$) was performed event-by-event using measurements of energy loss, time of flight, magnetic rigidity, and total kinetic energy. These measurements, combined with previous $^{82}$Se fragmentation data, were analyzed using an abrasion-ablation formalism and the recently developed $\Delta BE$ systematics. Model dependence in both approaches was quantified through a Bayesian-inspired model averaging procedure based on eleven nuclear mass models. The $\Delta BE$ systematics provide a simple means of incorporating nuclear structure information into production-rate predictions, while the abrasion-ablation analysis provides insight into the reaction mechanisms governing the production of neutron-rich nuclei. The production cross section predictions of these two approaches are in agreement for nuclei predicted to be well-bound by the mass models. Discrepancies between the two frameworks are large for nuclei near $N=48$, corresponding to pure-$Z$ removal. The agreement of $\Delta BE_{\mathrm{sys}}$ with the experimental data and the under-prediction of the AA calculations point to a potentially incomplete description of the reaction mechanism governing the production of these isotopes. The first observation of $^{71}$Cr provides an out-of-sample test of the predictive capability of the $\Delta BE$ systematics: a cross section of $1.94\times 10^{-13}$ mb, predicted using the HFB-22 mass table and $\Delta BE_{\mathrm{sys}}$ coefficients determined before the observation of $^{71}$Cr, is consistent with the measured value reported here: $2.20^{+2.10}_{-0.75}\times10^{-13}$ mb.

title: Research on Actinide Fission Yields: A Physics-informed Data-driven Approach
abstract: Abstract To address the need for accurate fission-yield data in applications such as r -process nucleosynthesis, and the limitations of existing models, this work proposes a physics-informed multimode fission-yield (PI-MFY) prediction model. The model is based on multimode fission theory and, adopting Bohr’s compound-nucleus independence hypothesis as a guiding assumption, constructs a four-dimensional physical feature space. Within this framework, an inverse-distance-weighted K -nearest-neighbors (IDW-KNN) algorithm is adopted to infer the model parameters nonparametrically from neighboring systems, enabling accurate predictions of the eight crucial parameters in multimode fission theory and subsequently yielding the corresponding pre-neutron-emission fission–fragment-mass distributions. Comparison of the calculated results of multiple fission systems with experimental data in the EXFOR database shows that the model achieves an RMSE of 0.00163 on the test set not involved in training, effectively avoiding overfitting and demonstrating good generalization capability. The model accurately reproduces the peak positions of the asymmetric bimodal structure arising from shell effects. Moreover, it exhibits greater flexibility than the traditional empirical formula and the general description of the fission observables (GEF) model in describing the energy dependence of the fission yields associated with the gradual damping of microscopic shell effects as the excitation energy increases. The present model is able to provide fission–fragment-mass distributions in good agreement with experimental data for fissioning systems that lie within or reasonably close to the experimentally covered nuclear region, thereby serving as a complementary approach to traditional methods. At this stage, however, the approach is more appropriately regarded as an auxiliary tool that provides a comparative reference for analyzing trends in fission–fragment-mass distributions in neutron-rich regions relevant to r -process nucleosynthesis.

title: Radiative decay and electromagnetic moments in Th 229 determined within nuclear density functional theory
abstract: Using the nuclear DFT approach with symmetry breaking and restoration, we investigate the electromagnetic properties of the ground and isomeric states in Th 229 . We determine the magnetic dipole transition strength B ( M 1 ; 3 / 2 1 + → 5 / 2 1 + ) between these two states along with their corresponding spectroscopic magnetic dipole, electric quadrupole, and magnetic octupole moments. We discuss the effects of parity breaking, configuration mixing, and time-odd core polarization. Because the octupole deformability of the standard Skyrme functionals varies, we analyze the results using a set of functionals and perform a regression aligned with the measured electric octupole moments of neighboring even-even nuclei. Without dedicated parameter adjustment, the results compare favorably with the experimental data but also indicate the need to systematically adjust the octupole degrees of freedom in future functional parametrizations.

title: Resolving the isospin-mixing anomaly in $^{26}$Si from $^{26}$P $\beta$-decay
abstract: The $\beta$-delayed one- and two-proton emission of the proton-dripline nucleus $^{26}$P provides a sensitive probe of isospin symmetry-breaking. A recent study reported the observation of a strongly isospin-mixed doublet in $^{26}$Si, comprised of the $T = 2$ Isobaric Analog State (IAS) and a state at 13380 keV, yielding a record-high isospin mixing matrix element. We report a new high-resolution measurement of the $^{26}$P $\beta$-delayed charged-particle decay performed at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB), shedding new light on the isospin mixing in this decay. By utilizing low-energy beam implantation from the Advanced Cryogenic Gas Stopper (ACGS), we obtained clean one-proton and two-proton decay spectra. Our high statistics study show discrepancies in decay branches and the existence of a 13380 keV state in $^{26}$Si is unsupported by our data. Our deduced branching ratio to the IAS is fully consistent with the expectation from the Fermi sum rule. Consequently, the claim of strong isospin mixing in $^{26}$Si is refuted, reinstating standard theoretical expectations for isospin mixing in nuclei.

title: Product units in gated recurrent networks enhance prediction of nuclear masses and charge radii
abstract: The prediction of nuclear properties using machine learning can complement theoretical models and advance the exploration of poorly known domains of the nuclear chart. We propose a machine learning technique for predicting nuclear masses and charge radii based on gated recurrent units (GRU) that integrates learnable product-unit mappings into the candidate state to model multiplicative dependencies among neighboring nuclei. Computations are performed in the complex domain to jointly capture amplitude and phase dynamics. Across three data partitions and three training seeds per partition, AM-PU-GRU achieves a mean mass interpolation RMSE of 0.2698 MeV and a temporal RMSE of 0.1905 MeV. Configuration comparisons support the integration of learned products into gated recurrence. Without mass inputs, MI-PU-GRU predicts charge radii with an RMSE of 0.019947 fm, 14.40% below the fixed WS* prior. Matched radius controls further show how candidate fusion shapes the benefit of learned products. Paired errors, nuclide-resolved maps, and inference measurements characterize predictive gains and computational cost. This article is an extended version of our ICCS 2026 conference paper (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-29921-5_10).

title: Impact of Effective Nucleon Mass and Symmetry Energy on Nuclear Pasta Phases and the Unified Equation of State of Neutron Stars
abstract: Abstract We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars. The nonuniform pasta structure is described within the self-consistent Thomas–Fermi approximation, while nucleonic interactions are treated in the relativistic mean-field framework with several typical parameter sets adopted. Our results indicate that the symmetry energy and its slope are crucial in determining the onset of pasta phases and their geometric configurations. In the high-density region where matter becomes uniform, the effective nucleon mass plays a dominant role. A larger effective nucleon mass tends to soften the EOS, which yields a smaller radius for a canonical 1.4 M ⊙ neutron star and reduces the corresponding tidal deformability.

title: Why magnetic-field effects are difficult to observe in relativistic heavy-ion collisions
abstract: Since a strong magnetic field is generated in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, novel phenomena have been predicted to occur in the quark-gluon plasma produced in these collisions. However, these predictions have not yet been convincingly confirmed experimentally. We reanalyze the generation and evolution of the magnetic field which plays a key role in the phenomena. Using the method of one-sided Fourier transformation, we reconcile the description in frequency and wave-vector space, which is required to properly account for the electromagnetic properties of the quark-gluon plasma, with the initial-value nature of the problem arising from the creation of the plasma medium at the moment of collision. We show that the currents induced in the quark-gluon plasma, which sustain the magnetic field, develop with a delay and are consequently less effective than usually assumed. Moreover, because the plasma initially consists predominantly of electrically neutral gluons, while charged quarks emerge at a later stage, the induced currents are further delayed. Consequently, a magnitude of the field present in the quark-gluon plasma is significantly lower than earlier estimates suggested. This may explain why magnetic-field effects are difficult to observe in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

title: Topology-based fast neutron background suppression and sterile-neutrino sensitivity in a segmented reactor ${\overline{\nu}}_{e}$ detector
abstract: Reactor electron antineutrinos are commonly detected through the inverse beta decay interaction, with a prompt positron followed by delayed neutron capture. In shallow or above-ground segmented organic scintillator detectors, correlated fast neutrons are a dominant background because proton recoils can mimic the prompt IBD signal. We study topology-based machine learning using the Indian Scintillator Matrix for Reactor Anti-Neutrinos detector as a case study. A multilayer perceptron is trained on reconstructed topological observables from detailed Geant4 simulations. The $\mathrm{F_{1}}$ score and bootstrap resampling on an independent validation sample yield a fixed threshold of $P{\mathrm{IBD}}>0.40$. Applied without further optimization to an independent testing sample, the MLP retains $\mathrm{(83.4\pm 0.7)\%}$ of IBD events and rejects $\mathrm{(77.3\pm 0.7)\%}$ of fast neutron events. In a controlled spectral benchmark using an independent AmBe fast neutron spectrum, the selection reduces the net candidate-spectrum deformation by $\mathrm{84\%}$. The energy dependent signal acceptance and residual fast neutron component are subsequently incorporated into a binned likelihood, which recovers the injected IBD signal strength as $\mathrm{\hat{\alpha}=0.993^{+0.053}_{-0.048}}$, with an empirical goodness-of-fit probability of $0.434$. The expected sterile-neutrino sensitivity for the ISMRAN detector is evaluated at baselines of 13 m and 18 m, with two years of exposure at each baseline. For the nominal pre-MLP $S/B=1:2$ benchmark and the background model, retaining the classifier score in a joint ($\mathrm{E_{prompt}\times P_{IBD}}$) likelihood improves the 95\% C.L. sensitivity to $\sin^{2}2\theta_{14}$ by a logarithmically averaged 7.9\% over $0.1\leq\Delta m_{41}^{2}\leq1~\mathrm{eV}^{2}$ relative to an energy-only likelihood with the same fast neutron contamination.

title: Sensitivity to $\Theta^+$ production in the $\pi^- p \to K^- X$ reaction at HIAF-HIRIBL
abstract: Pion-induced searches for the $\Theta^+$ can probe the proposed $N^*(2400)$ formation region beyond the E19 energies. We present sensitivity projections for a missing-mass search for a narrow $\Theta^+$ at 1.540 GeV/$c^2$ in $\pi^- p \to K^- X$ at the High Intensity heavy-ion Accelerator Facility and its HIgh-rigidity Radioactive Ion Beam Line. With the E19 resolutions, efficiency, and continuum, separate 10-day exposures at pion momenta of 2.01 and 2.586 GeV/$c$ give background-only median expected 90% CL upper limits of 0.0293 and 0.0356 $\mu$b/sr, respectively, on the differential cross section averaged over $2^\circ$ to $15^\circ$ on the selected high-momentum branch; the higher momentum corresponds to the proposed $N^*(2400)$ formation energy. Median local $5\sigma$ discovery thresholds are 0.0894 and 0.109 $\mu$b/sr. Nonresonant nucleon-exchange models give width scales of 0.0039 to 0.079 MeV for $J^P=1/2^+$ and 0.045 to 1.47 MeV for $J^P=1/2^-$. All positive-parity variants would test the DIANA width scale of $0.34 \pm 0.10$ MeV; negative-parity sensitivity depends on the variant.

title: Multipolar neutrino radiation in binary neutron star mergers: Angular structure, rotational variability, and implications for electron fraction
abstract: The angular structure and temporal variability of neutrino emission from binary neutron star mergers are characterized using fully general-relativistic simulations with energy-integrated M1 neutrino transport across a representative set of equations of state, total masses and mass ratios. The main analysis is restricted to merger remnants that do not collapse to a black hole within the simulated time intervals. The angle-dependent neutrino energy flux is extracted on a spherical surface outside the remnant and decomposed into spherical harmonics to quantify its multipolar content and evolution. Following the initial post-merger transient, the neutrino radiation flux approaches an axisymmetric configuration dominated by a strong quadrupolar component, producing persistent polar flux enhancement and equatorial suppression due to torus shadowing. The dipolar contribution remains subdominant, indicating the absence of sustained one-sided emission. The degree of anisotropy increases with mass asymmetry and for softer equations of state, reflecting the compactness and morphology of the remnant--disk system. Superimposed on this time-averaged geometry, coherent azimuthal modulations associated with the $m=1$ mode are identified. The associated half frequency, $f_{\mathrm{dom}}/2\simeq0.6$--$0.7\,\mathrm{kHz}$, is compared with local rotation rates in the simulated remnant--disk systems, suggesting a possible dynamical association between the remnant structure and neutrino variability. Finally, we quantify how the same quadrupole-dominated radiation geometry induces a latitude-dependent equilibrium electron fraction. The polar material is driven close to the neutrino-equilibrium target, whereas equatorial material remains systematically more neutron rich and below equilibrium.

versions.title: Multipolar neutrino radiation in binary neutron star mergers: Angular structure, rotational variability, and implications for electron fraction
versions.abstract: The angular structure and temporal variability of neutrino emission from binary neutron star mergers are characterized using fully general-relativistic simulations with energy-integrated M1 neutrino transport across a representative set of equations of state, total masses and mass ratios. The main analysis is restricted to merger remnants that do not collapse to a black hole within the simulated time intervals. The angle-dependent neutrino energy flux is extracted on a spherical surface outside the remnant and decomposed into spherical harmonics to quantify its multipolar content and evolution. Following the initial post-merger transient, the neutrino radiation flux approaches an axisymmetric configuration dominated by a strong quadrupolar component, producing persistent polar flux enhancement and equatorial suppression due to torus shadowing. The dipolar contribution remains subdominant, indicating the absence of sustained one-sided emission. The degree of anisotropy increases with mass asymmetry and for softer equations of state, reflecting the compactness and morphology of the remnant--disk system. Superimposed on this time-averaged geometry, coherent azimuthal modulations associated with the $m=1$ mode are identified. The associated half frequency, $f_{\mathrm{dom}}/2\simeq0.6$--$0.7\,\mathrm{kHz}$, is compared with local rotation rates in the simulated remnant--disk systems, suggesting a possible dynamical association between the remnant structure and neutrino variability. title: Knowledge-guided machine learning deciphers spatiotemporal dynamics in chemical reactor systems
abstract: Characterizing the spatiotemporal dynamics of complex chemical reactors, especially localized engineering-critical points or regions, remains challenging in process engineering. Although data-driven methods offer computational advantages, the incorporation of domain-specific physical knowledge can further enhance their predictive performance. Here, we present a physics-informed machine learning framework that systematically embeds coking mechanisms and heat transfer principles into neural network architecture and training constraints. Using a coke-accumulating cracking reactor as a prototypical case, the proposed approach reproduces the spatiotemporal distributions of key operational parameters obtained from conventional simulations with high fidelity and achieves a 105-fold computational acceleration. Crucially, the incorporation of mechanistic knowledge enhances prediction fidelity for critical safety indicators, particularly the maximum external wall temperature (error < 0.5%), enabling precise identification of optimal decoking intervals. This paradigm bridges data efficiency with domain-informed modeling, providing a useful reference for developing real-time monitoring and optimization models for complex industrial systems. A physics-informed neural network embeds coking and heat transfer knowledge via an output integration layer and region-weighted loss to predict reactor spatiotemporal fields; it matches conventional simulation results, improves peak wall temperature accuracy, and runs about five orders of magnitude faster than conventional simulations.

title: Is XTE J1814-338 a dark matter-admixed neutron star?
abstract: We explore the possibility that the ultracompact object XTE J1814-338 is a dark matter-admixed neutron star (DNS) based on a general-relativistic two-fluid approach, in which one fluid describes ordinary nuclear matter and the other dark matter. The equations of state of nuclear matter and dark matter are described by the Brueckner-Hartree-Fock (BHF) theory with realistic three-body forces and a generic bosonic self-interacting dark matter model, respectively. Based on the observational data, we determine the parameter space for XTE J1814-338 as a DNS, and find that only a halo stellar configuration with a high dark matter fraction is allowed. Furthermore, we predict other observable properties of XTE J1814-338 and provide robust lower bounds for these quantities.

title: Experimental and numerical investigation of backstreaming positive ions in an RF-driven negative ion source
abstract: Abstract Backstreaming positive ions are an unavoidable byproduct in high-power negative ion-based neutral beam injection systems, posing a critical challenge to the long-pulse operational stability of ion sources due to the significant heat loads and material erosion they induce. This paper presents a comprehensive experimental and numerical investigation into the generation, spatial distribution, and thermal effects of BSPIs in the dual-RF-driver negative ion source at the HONOR test facility of CRAFT. Using a water-flow calorimetry diagnostic system, the dependence of the Backstreaming positive ion power fraction (PBSPI/Pbeam) on key operational parameters was systematically studied. The results show that the PBSPI/Pbeam ratio increases monotonically with the source filling pressure, rising from ~2.05% at 0.3 Pa to ~3.15% at 0.57 Pa. A non-monotonic dependence on beam energy is observed, with the ratio peaking at ~2.65% at 161 keV. This trend is attributed to the competition between the improved geometric transmission efficiency of BSPIs—resulting from reduced beam divergence at moderate energies—and the intrinsic decrease in collision cross-sections at higher energies. Furthermore, the ratio is found to decrease with increasing extracted beam current, which is explained by the space-charge-induced beam divergence that reduces the geometric transmission efficiency through the acceleration grids. Distinct BSPI bombardment traces on the backplate exhibit an array pattern corresponding to the plasma grid apertures. Coupled thermal-fluid-solid simulations, incorporating the measured heat loads, indicate that under typical high-power conditions (190 kV, 16.2 A), the maximum backplate temperature remains well below the material safety limit. This work clarifies the key mechanisms governing BSPI generation and validates the thermal reliability of the backplate design, providing a solid basis for the development of high-power NNBI systems.

title: Confinement property in the JT-60SA first operation phase
abstract: Abstract In JT-60SA, the global energy confinement time τ E has been evaluated to be 0.1-0.2 s for 1 MA hydrogen discharges and compared with the ITERL-96P(th) scaling. Because local measurements of ion temperature T i , electron density and effective charge are not available in the first operation phase and the number of discharges and their parameter range are limited, the present results should not be considered definitive. As heating power increased, τ E tends to shorten in the same trend as the scaling. τ E is shorter than the scaling but approaches the scaling with increasing density. For 0.4-0.6 MW ohmic heating plasmas, τ E increases with increasing collisionality and saturates. For 0.6-0.8 MW ohmic heating and electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECH) plasmas, τ E continues to increase up to higher collisionality and reaches the scaling. The turbulence simulations with the trapped gyroLandau-fluid model assuming a linear T i profile show that the dominant turbulence mode is trapped electron modes. The linear growth rate decreases with increasing collisionality and saturates at a low level in the 0.4-0.6 MW ohmic heating plasma, suggesting the transition from the linear ohmic confinement regime to the saturated ohmic confinement regime. For 0.6-0.8 MW ohmic heating and ECH plasmas, the saturation occurs at higher collisionality, indicating that the linear confinement regime extends to higher collisionality. The global particle confinement time excluding recycling contributions, τ p , has also been evaluated to be 0.301±0.015 s, approximately twice τ E , from the frequency responses in a density feedback control experiment. From τ p and the effective particle confinement time including recycling τ p * , a recycling coefficient is obtained as 0.865±0.013. The sub-unity recycling coefficient indicates that wall recycling is insufficient to maintain plasma density, consistent with hydrogen retention due to the first hydrogen discharge with continuous gas injection.

title: A short-range effective theory for single-neutron halo nuclei with a deformed core
abstract: Abstract We establish a short-range effective theory for deformed s-wave halos. The theory applies to a system in which neutrons are weakly bound to a core nucleus, and that core nucleus also exhibits a low-lying rotational band with a 0 + ground state and a first 2 + 1 excited state. The effective theory then must have both halo degrees of freedom and degrees of freedom associated with rotation of the core. This leads to the particle plus rotor model of Bohr and Mottelson at leading order. We identify the relevant leading-order operators in the Hamiltonian that respect the symmetries of the system and the small parameters which define the effective theory's power counting. We carry out calculations for the 11 Be and 17 C systems in which we compute the low-lying positiveparity states of the core + neutron systems up to the core(2 + 1 )-neutron threshold. We do this for several different regulator parameters and establish that these energies can be renormalized using the leading-order set of operators. The spectrum is accurately described at leading order in both cases. Decay widths to d-wave core-neutron states have sizable cutoff dependence, but the Asymptotic Normalization Coefficients (ANCs) in s-wave channels exhibit regulator dependence of a size consistent with next-to-leading-order effects. We also compute Coulomb breakup observables and compare with experimental data, finding leading-order results in reasonable agreement with data for both 11 Be and 17 C. The addition of one next-to-leading-order operator renders the ANCs of all s-wave states stable with respect to the regulator. It consequently also removes most of the 30% variation of the leading-order Coulomb dissociation cross section with the regulator.
journal_abbrev: J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys.

title: Design of a low-level rf-based adaptive mode-0 feedback system for storage rings
abstract: The longitudinal coupled-bunch mode-0 instability is a significant collective effect in high-current storage rings. It appears as a coherent oscillation of the common synchrotron phase and energy deviation of multiple bunches, causing jitter in bunch arrival time and beam energy and thereby degrading timing stability, longitudinal beam quality, and the achievable stored current. Conventional mode-0 feedback systems typically use dedicated narrowband cavity filters to extract the mode-0 oscillation component and introduce a phase-shifting stage to establish the quadrature phase relation required for damping. Although effective, such implementations rely on dedicated cavity-filter hardware, which increases system integration complexity and cost. In addition, variations in the synchrotron oscillation frequency require feedback-phase adjustments to maintain optimum damping. To address these limitations, we propose a cavity-filter-free adaptive mode-0 feedback method based on the low-level rf (LLRF) system. In this method, the mode-0 component is extracted in the FPGA using digital algorithms and adaptively phase-shifted using a zero-padded FFT spectral-peak tracking algorithm. The phase-shifted signal is applied through a rotation-matrix operation in the vector modulator, providing damping of the mode-0 synchrotron oscillation via rf phase modulation. To verify the feasibility of the algorithm under no-beam conditions, an LLRF test platform was developed using parameters of the Super Tau-Charm Facility (STCF). The platform generates an equivalent BPM sum signal and implements discrete rf-cavity and beam phase-response models in the FPGA to form a self-contained closed loop. Offline tests show that, when the power levels of the first-order revolution sideband and the mode-0 oscillation sideband are − 3.96 and − 36.49 dBc relative to the rf carrier, respectively, the system extracts a mode-0 oscillation component with a spectral peak approximately 70 dB above the noise floor. The feedback loop effectively suppresses the mode-0 sideband. For five prescribed synchrotron-oscillation frequencies, the proposed zero-padded FFT spectral-peak tracking algorithm reduces the required data-acquisition time by approximately a factor of 85 compared with a conventional FFT at the same frequency resolution, while limiting the frequency-tracking error to below 1%. The maximum deviation between the additional feedback phase calculated by the algorithm and the optimum feedback phase obtained from the manual phase scan is less than 4 ° , demonstrating low-latency adaptive phase adjustment for varying synchrotron-oscillation-frequency conditions.

title: MR-ToF-assisted In-Source Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy at IGISOL
abstract: Multi-Reflection Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometer (MR-ToF-MS) assisted in-source laser resonance ionization spectroscopy (RIS) has been implemented at the Ion Guide Isotope Separator On-Line (IGISOL) facility, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a. Exotic nuclei, produced via fusion-evaporation reactions, are stopped and neutralized in a hot-cavity catcher, and selectively laser-ionized through a multi-step resonance ionization scheme before being transported to the MR-ToF-MS device. This combination of techniques is aimed at optically probing the very exotic N=Z nuclei in the immediate vicinity of $^{100}$Sn. The laser system, hot-cavity ion source, isobaric purification and detection stages are described. A representative hyperfine-structure spectrum of the proton-rich silver isotope $^{101}$Ag is presented as a case example.

title: Low- T / | W | instabilities in differentially rotating neutron stars resembling merger remnants
abstract: We construct constant rest-mass sequences of equilibrium models of differentially rotating neutron stars which resemble binary neutron star post-merger remnants. For a more realistic description of the post-merger remnant, we impose that each model carries approximately $95\%$ of the angular momentum that a binary system with the same total rest-mass has at the moment of merging, based on an empirical relation informed from neutron star merger simulations. We account for equation of state effects by employing two distinct microphysical descriptions for high density matter. We dynamically evolve the equilibrium models with a three-dimensional general relativistic hydrodynamics code that employs the conformal flatness approximation. We investigate the connection between the occurrence of the instability and the existence of corotation radii within the stellar configurations and determine the instability window for both equation of state sequences. The occurrence of low-$T/|W|$ instabilities leads to pronounced gravitational wave emission in the range $0.13 \lessapprox\beta \lessapprox 0.2$, while models outside this range exhibit less pronounced features in the gravitational wave spectrum. The prominence of gravitational wave emission is primarily determined by $\beta$, while the equation of state seems to have a more minor effect. We present correlations between the strength of the gravitational wave emission associated with the instability and properties of the equilibrium models. Stellar configurations modelled by different equations of state display differences in the timescales over which the various dynamical features develop, as well as whether they exhibit a pronounced $m=1$ deformation. Potential relations between the instability growth timescales and properties of the stellar models are studied.

title: Gaia DR3 Compact Binary Candidates Constrained by Radial Velocity Measurements
abstract: Abstract Astrometry enables the most direct determination of the orbital elements and component masses of compact binaries. The potential of the current Gaia data for this purpose has not yet been fully explored. In this work, we combine Gaia astrometric and radial velocity (RV) measurements to perform joint orbital fitting for 1835 Gaia astrometric binaries with available RV data. Among the 518 systems with at least three effective RV epochs, we identify 171 compact binary candidates, including four with inferred dark companion masses exceeding 2.1 M ⊙ and 22 between 1.4 and 2.1 M ⊙ . These candidates provide valuable targets for future follow-up observations and Gaia DR4 analyses. We also flag 1317 additional potential compact binary candidates with effective RV epochs less than three, including 84 with inferred companion masses above 2.1 M ⊙ and 173 between 1.4 and 2.1 M ⊙ . More importantly, our results point to a large, currently hidden population of black hole and neutron star binaries that can be further explored with the forthcoming Gaia DR4 data and complementary follow-up observations.

title: Artificial Intelligence for VAMOS++: From Data Analysis to Intelligent Instrumentation
abstract: The increasing complexity of nuclear-physics experiments calls for analysis methods that combine precision, efficiency, and reproducibility. This article reviews the integration of artificial intelligence into the analysis framework of the VAMOS++ large-acceptance magnetic spectrometer at GANIL and discusses its evolution toward intelligent instrumentation. Deep neural networks exploit nonlinear correlations between detector observables to reconstruct ion trajectories and identify atomic charge states and atomic numbers. These approaches achieve performance comparable to or better than conventional methods while substantially reducing manual intervention and processing time. Trajectory reconstruction reaches processing rates of millions of events per second, while particle identification using fractionally labelled events reduces analysis procedures from months or years to minutes. These advances support high-resolution isotopic identification and facilitate consistent analysis across experimental campaigns, benefiting nuclear structure, reaction dynamics, and fission studies. Ongoing developments extend this framework to detector self-calibration, using experimental data and physical constraints to determine detector responses with reduced reliance on dedicated calibration measurements or labelled reference datasets. Applications to segmented ionization chambers and tracking detectors illustrate the potential for integrating calibration, reconstruction, and performance monitoring. Together, these developments outline a path toward adaptive, self-optimizing instrumentation that can respond to changing experimental conditions and increase the scientific return of complex nuclear-physics experiments.

title: Second order and secondary functional renormalization group flow equations
abstract: The functional renormalization group provides a powerful non-perturbative framework for quantum field theory through the exact flow equation for the scale-dependent effective action. A mass-type regulator $R_k = k^2$ is particularly attractive because it preserves symmetries, locality, and unitarity (or Osterwalder--Schrader reflection positivity in the Euclidean domain). However, unlike momentum-dependent regulators, it does not tame all ultraviolet divergences: in four dimensions, flow equations for the effective potential exhibit logarithmic divergences. Motivated by Callan's perturbative renormalization scheme, where higher-order $\theta$-insertions improve ultraviolet convergence, we develop two classes of higher-order functional flow equations. First, we derive exact second-order flow equations by taking further derivatives of the standard flow equation with respect to $k$. These have either a one-loop structure involving the first derivative of the inverse propagator, or a mixed one-loop and two-loop structure. While exact and useful for incorporating two-loop effects and testing truncation schemes, they do not in general resolve the ultraviolet convergence problem. Second, we introduce a secondary flow method, where variations of an effective mass-squared parameter introduce an additional flow, with parameter $l$. The resulting secondary flow equations become ultraviolet finite once sufficiently many derivatives have been taken, and can be evaluated without an additional ultraviolet regulator. Integrating back to the standard flow requires integration constants that encode microscopic ultraviolet physics, analogous to relevant coupling constants.

title: Real-time simulation of scattering in $\phi^4$ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts
abstract: Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in $\phi^4$ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulation of scattering.

title: Early-time dynamics of heavy-ion collisions through energy correlators: Celestial blocks and the spacetime structure of out-of-equilibrium QCD matter
abstract: Ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions provide a unique window into far-from-equilibrium states of QCD matter. The initial stages of these events are characterized by highly anisotropic, nonthermal dynamics that precede hydrodynamization, yet they remain largely inaccessible through conventional soft observables. In this work, we show that the substructure of midrapidity jets provides direct sensitivity to the spacetime structure of this early, anisotropic phase. Using classical Yang-Mills simulations and effective kinetic theory to model the early time evolution of the jet quenching parameter, we compute the contribution of a single g → c c ¯ splitting to the azimuthally differential energy-energy correlator within the Baier-Dokshitzer-Mueller-Peigné-Schiff-Zakharov (BDMPS-Z) framework, as a controlled proof of principle. By decomposing the result into celestial blocks, we isolate the coefficients that encode the anisotropic geometry and dynamics of the underlying medium. We identify an observable that couples directly to spatial anisotropies in the out-of-equilibrium QCD matter and also discuss the impact of medium response on its behavior. We further extend our study to midrapidity jets generated with the Monte-Carlo, adjusted to incorporate an anisotropic medium background, and find that the observable remains sensitive to directional medium effects at the level of reconstructed jets, providing a complementary test of the effect identified analytically and motivating experimental searches for azimuthal jet substructure as a probe of the early time anisotropic matter. Finally, we discuss how higher-point energy correlators and generalized energy-flow operators can enhance the sensitivity to the microscopic structure of far-from-equilibrium QCD matter.

title: Are hybrid hydrodynamic models missing soft-pion physics?
abstract: In this work, we perform a systematic Bayesian analysis of the full parameter space of a state-of-the-art hybrid hydrodynamical model and show that no combination of parameters provides a satisfactory description of the low-$p_T$ region of the pion $(\pi^{\pm})$ transverse-momentum spectra. This suggests that an additional mechanism enhancing pion production at low $p_T$ may be needed to properly describe the ALICE data. We first reexamine and confirm the existence of an excess of low $p_T$ pions relative to model predictions, showing that no comparable excess is observed in the spectra of kaons $(K^\pm)$, protons $(p)$, or antiprotons $(\bar{p})$. We further demonstrate that this excess persists under a rigorous Bayesian analysis of simulations that include, e.g., a hadronic afterburner, a feature omitted in previous similar studies. Despite the observed excess, the scaled pion spectra retain their universal behavior, exhibiting little dependence on collision centrality. In fact, pions exhibit the most pronounced universality among the particle species considered. We then estimate the effects of two candidate mechanisms for generating the low-$p_T$ pion enhancement by introducing a one-parameter extension of the model into the Bayesian analysis. We find that the data favor enhancement mechanisms whose contributions decrease with increasing $p_T$, becoming negligible at high-$p_T$. Our results motivate further investigations of non-equilibrium effects in hybrid hydrodynamic simulations.

title: A Numerical Investigation of Oxygen Ion Escape from Ancient Earth: Influences of Magnetic Dipole Moment and Dipole Tilt Angle
abstract: Abstract Earth ionospheric oxygen ions (O + ) escaping into interplanetary space, the Earth wind, represent a critical mechanism in Earth’s long-term atmospheric evolution. The geomagnetic field, whose dipole moment strength and orientation have varied significantly throughout geologic history, is considered a primary factor controlling this escape. Accurate assessment of atmospheric evolution requires systematic study of O + escape across diverse geomagnetic configurations. In this study, we develop a global 3D multifluid magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model within the BATS-R-US framework, self-consistently tracing H + and O + as separate ion fluids coupled through ion–neutral collisions and photochemical reactions. Under typical solar wind conditions, we examine how dipole moment strength and tilt angle modulate the O + escape rate. The results show the following: (1) The dipole moment strength is the dominant control on O + escape. As the field weakens, the escape rate exhibits pronounced nonlinear growth. At 10 −1 times the present-day value, the escape rate increases by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude; below 10 −2 , it approaches saturation at ∼10 25 –10 26 s −1 , limited by the ionospheric source. (2) The dipole tilt angle provides secondary modulation at fixed field strength, primarily by altering the geometry of solar wind–magnetosphere coupling and cusp exposure, producing a variation of more than 3 times across the full angular range. (3) Under extreme paleomagnetic conditions such as geomagnetic reversals, the collapse of the dipole moment—rather than the dipole tilt—drives heavy-ion escape upward by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude, creating episodic windows of enhanced atmospheric loss. These results provide quantitative constraints on Earth wind variability under changing geomagnetic conditions.

title: Self-Consistent Subtracted Second Quasiparticle Random-Phase Approximation for Dipole Responses in Neutron-Rich Oxygen Isotopes
abstract: Describing the nuclear dipole response in open-shell nuclei across wide energy scales, from low-lying states below the neutron separation energy to giant resonances near 30MeV, within a single microscopic framework is a long-standing open problem. Here we establish, for the first time, a self-consistent subtracted second quasiparticle random-phase approximation (SSQRPA) that simultaneously incorporates pairing correlations (HF+BCS), explicit two-quasiparticle (2qp) and four-quasiparticle (4qp) configurations in a large model space, the full forward- and backward-going QRPA structure, and a subtraction procedure to eliminate double counting and ensure stability. No existing framework unifies all of these ingredients in the quasiparticle basis. We apply SSQRPA to the dipole excitations of neutron-rich oxygen isotopes $^{18,20,22}$O, where the standard QRPA fails to simultaneously account for high-energy giant dipole resonance (GDR) states near 22--25MeV, medium-energy GDR states in the 10--18MeV region, and isolated low-lying $1^-$ states below the neutron separation energy. In SSQRPA, the dominant isovector (IV) GDR strength shifts downward by approximately 4MeV into the experimentally observed medium-energy region, while the compressional isoscalar (IS) GDR strength remains concentrated at higher energies, in qualitative agreement with the observed electromagnetic dissociation cross sections. For the low-lying states, the root-mean-square deviation from experiment is reduced from 5.31MeV (QRPA) to 0.35MeV (SSQRPA) in $^{18}$O, and from 4.07MeV to 0.74MeV in $^{20}$O, demonstrating that 4qp correlations are essential for a simultaneous description of dipole excitations over a wide range of excitation energies. The SSQRPA provides a powerful and general framework for future microscopic studies of collective excitations in open-shell nuclei across the nuclear mass table.

title: Real-time Electron Tagging by Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy in the PTOLEMY experiment
abstract: The PTOLEMY project aims at measuring the neutrino mass and, in the future, the Cosmic Neutrino Background from Tritium endpoint measurement. The Radio-Frequency (RF) Tracker is a sub-detector with the goal of measuring in real time the electrons by exploiting the Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy. In this work, an overview of the PTOLEMY project is given together with the design, simulation, construction and commissioning of the RF Tracker prototype: the Electron Trap. The measurements and data analysis of the Electron Trap are presented, establishing the primary path for the development of the RF Tracker.

title: On the origin and geometry of anomaly-related poles in Double Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering
abstract: Anomaly-related poles have been reported in one-loop box amplitudes for the gluon-initiated channel of double deeply virtual Compton scattering (DDVCS). The residues of these poles carry the gluonic operator structures associated with the chiral and trace anomalies. The origin of the poles within the box amplitude has remained unclear. In this work, we trace both poles to a subleading Landau singularity on the boundary of the box's Feynman-parameter domain, where one parameter vanishes and the remaining three propagators form a triangle subdiagram. We examine the same boundary using dimensional regularization (DR), nonzero momentum transfer $t$, and a finite quark mass $m$. At $t=m=0$, the boundary contribution is power infrared divergent in four dimensions. Analytic continuation in DR conceals this divergence, which gives no $1/\epsilon$ pole about $d=4$. At the critical dimension $d=6$, the same endpoint diverges logarithmically and gives a pole in the continued integral. Nonzero $t$ and finite $m$ regulate the same boundary region, yielding the known anomaly-related $1/t$ pole and a previously unreported $1/m^2$ behavior, respectively. We also show that a transverse gluon-polarization projector can eliminate an anomaly-related contribution that survives with explicit gluon polarization vectors. Finally, we present complete one-loop results for polarized and unpolarized DDVCS with all three infrared prescriptions. After summing the diagrams, the same evolution kernel governs the infrared pole in DR and the logarithms $\ln(Q^2/(-t))$ and $\ln(Q^2/m^2)$ within each polarization channel. This work establishes the common geometric origin of these anomaly-related poles within one-loop box amplitudes.

title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
abstract: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.

title: MID: a muon detector for the ALICE 3 upgrade project
abstract: The success of the ALICE programme has allowed to study the hottest state of matter created in the laboratory: the strongly-interacting quark-gluon plasma (sQGP). However, some fundamental questions on the sQGP and other aspects of the strong interaction will remain open even after LHC Run 4. To address this, the ALICE collaboration has proposed a major upgrade of its detector, known as ALICE 3. Among the subdetectors considered for this upgrade is the muon identification detector (MID), whose aim is to contribute to the study of charmonium and exotic-hadron production in heavy-ion collisions. While the baseline design consists of plastic-scintillator-based chambers placed around a cylindrical magnetic iron absorber, different detector technologies are under evaluation for the MID, including multi-wire proportional chambers. This proceeding presents the results of two MID prototypes based on FNAL-NICADD scintillator bars, Kuraray fibers and Hamamatsu SiPMs, characterized in test beams at the CERN Proton Synchrotron with 3 GeV/$c$ muon- and pion-enriched beams. The muon efficiency as well as the hadron suppression obtained using machine learning techniques will be discussed.
authors: Jesus Eduardo Mu\~noz Mendez (for the ALICE Collaboration)

Searching for signatures of criticality in heavy-ion collisions using two-pion correlation functions
abstract: We study possible signatures of the existence of a Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) critical end-point in low-energy relativistic heavy-ion collisions using two-pion femtoscopy. We simulate central $^{209}\mathrm{Bi}+^{209}\mathrm{Bi}$ collisions at center-of-mass energies ranging from $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.8$ to 11 GeV using the EPOS 4.0.3 framework, incorporating an equation of state that explicitly includes a critical end-point and is compatible with lattice QCD results at small baryon chemical potentials. We analyze the pion pair-distance distribution and the corresponding two-pion correlation function by fitting them with L\'evy distributions in configuration and momentum spaces, respectively. We find a weak dependence of the source parameters on the collision energy below $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=9.2$ GeV, followed by a change in trend at higher energies, particularly in the intercept parameter $\lambda$. This behavior may be associated with a decreasing fraction of pions coming from the core and an increasing contribution from long-lived resonance decays. Within the present analysis, we do not identify an unambiguous signal attributable to the critical end-point. A comparison with simulations employing different equation of state parameters to vary the strength of the critical point, as well as with simulations without a critical end-point, is necessary to establish the sensitivity of these observables to critical phenomena.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

title: n = 1 ideal MHD stability of tokamak plasmas with low aspect ratio and negative triangularity
abstract: Abstract Spherical tokamaks (STs) exhibit good ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) stability owing to their low-aspect-ratio configuration, while negative triangularity (NT) configurations have recently attracted considerable attention for their superior confinement performance, despite their inferior MHD stability. To evaluate whether these two advantageous regimes can be reconciled, we investigate the n = 1 ideal no-wall MHD stability of NT configurations at low aspect ratios. Using the CHEASE+MARS code suite, we perform beta limit scans over various triangularity and aspect ratio values, with prescribed safety factor q profiles and normalized pressure gradient p ′ profiles, which provides a controlled comparison. The results show that, at lower aspect ratios, the stability of positive triangularity (PT) configurations is enhanced, consistent with classical expectations; whereas counter-intuitively, the stability of NT configurations deteriorates. We present several physical interpretations of this phenomenon, both qualitatively (‘good/bad curvature’) and quantitatively (magnetic well depth and Mercier criterion), and show that they are consistent with the calculated trend. In addition, the stabilizing effect of the safety factor is preserved at low aspect ratios for both PT and NT configurations, partially mitigating the aforementioned stability deterioration of NT plasmas.

title: Two-dimensional transport mechanisms in the vicinity of the X-points in snowflake divertors
abstract: Abstract Snowflake divertor (SFD) experiments show enhanced radial transport near the X-points, more than may be explained by standard two-dimensional edge transport models without drifts. Here we investigate transport mechanisms in SFDs through two complementary approaches: (i) modelling of recent SFD experiments performed at MAST-U with the edge transport code UEDGE with E × B and ∇ B drifts enabled, and (ii) reduced modelling of transport and turbulence in the vicinity of the X-points with a model developed here and implemented in BOUT++. Through these two approaches we assess the two leading candidates for this transport: equilibrium E × B drifts driven by strong poloidal gradients near the primary X-point, and the ‘churning mode’ (CM), a toroidally-symmetric plasma vortex close to the X-points. UEDGE modelling shows that equilibrium E × B drifts do play a role in increasing particle and energy transport across the primary separatrix, increasing the proportion of heat flux delivered to secondary strike points (SPs) and reducing peak heat fluxes at the primary SPs. This mechanism is less effective in the upper divertor due the reversed drift directions in combination with the device geometry. Including drifts in the model is also shown to improve agreement with the experimental radiated power profiles. To self-consistently compare the impact of drifts and the CM we develop a reduced-MHD model which includes both effects, and which is implemented in BOUT++. We find that equilibrium E × B drifts are dominant when the ratio of plasma pressure in the null region to poloidal magnetic pressure at the midplane is low, β pm ≲ 0.5 − 1.0 % , which were the conditions obtained in the MAST-U experiments. The CM was found to be dominant for β pm ≳ 1.0 , leading to increased transport across the null region and activation of secondary divertor legs.

title: On the electromagnetic effects of collisionless trapped-electron modes
abstract: Abstract We present a linear gyrokinetic theory for the electromagnetic collisionless trapped-electron mode (CTEM). It is found that the weak electromagnetic effects of CTEMs originate from the particle dynamics. Theoretical analysis reveals that the kinetic and fluid-like components of the trapped-electron parallel current cancel at leading order. The ion parallel current is also negligible due to the weak ion transit resonance. Consequently, the perturbed parallel current in the electromagnetic CTEM is dominated by passing electrons. We demonstrate that these characteristic particle dynamics decouple the CTEM from the shear Alfv'en wave branch at leading order, thereby rendering the electromagnetic effects subdominant. Both eigenmode analyses and gyrokinetic simulations validate these findings.

title: Numerical evaluation of Paschen-α Zeeman spectroscopy for recombination front position measurement in JT-60SA detached divertor plasma
abstract: Abstract This study numerically evaluates the feasibility of measuring the deuterium recombination front position, which serves as an indicator of plasma detachment, using the Zeeman effect on the deuterium Paschen-α line spectrum observed along a few viewing chords in the JT-60SA divertor. The position is inferred by correlating the known magnetic field distribution along the viewing chord with the magnetic field strength deduced from the Zeeman effect of the Paschen-α line. Detached and attached plasmas with argon and neon gas injection are simulated using the integrated divertor code SONIC, and synthetic Paschen-α line spectra in the detached plasmas are computed by incorporating Stark, Doppler, and instrumental broadenings. The blackbody radiation intensity, which affects Paα line spectroscopy as a statistical error, is evaluated using the target plate temperature obtained from a heat conduction simulation. Regression analysis based on a point-emission model reproduces the chord-integrated spectra and yields the recombination front position within 1.23 cm of the actual position. The result indicates the potential of Zeeman spectroscopy of the Paschen-α line as a means of diagnosing the recombination front using only a few viewing chords.

title: Multiphysics modelling of molten salt blankets for ARC-class fusion reactors
abstract: Abstract This work presents a multiphysics modelling framework for liquid molten-salt blankets in ARC-class fusion reactors. The model couples magnetohydrodynamics, turbulent heat transfer, and neutron-photon transport within a unified computational environment. The framework is implemented in nemoFoam, an OpenFOAM-based multiphysics platform previously developed for deterministic neutron-photon transport and thermal-hydraulics; extended in the present work with MHD equations and turbulence closures. Turbulence is modelled using standard and cubic k-ε closures, both in their baseline formulations and in variants modified to account for MHD effects following the approach proposed by Meng. Results indicate that standard turbulence closures become unreliable under strong magnetic fields, as they tend to overpredict turbulence production and therefore turbulent transport. Moreover, linear eddy-viscosity models cannot represent secondary-flow structures that control local mixing and heat transfer in complex blanket geometries. For these reasons, the modified cubic k-ε model, combining an anisotropic stress-strain relationship with MHD damping, seems to provide a physically more complete representation of the flow across the ARC breeding-blanket domain than the other closures examined, although a definitive assessment would require dedicated experimental validation for geometries of this type. The results highlight the need for turbulence closures that remain robust from inertia-dominated channels to magnetically dominated tank regions.

title: A trap-based platform for cooling and laser spectroscopy of fast ions toward radioactive-ion applications
abstract: We report on the first experiments with the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) segmented linear Paul trap. The intent for this apparatus is to serve as an efficient capture and laser-cooling trap for radioactive isotopes produced at radioactive ion beam facilities. We demonstrate the deceleration of 10 keV ion beams and their trapping and laser cooling into Coulomb crystals. As an initial spectroscopic benchmark, the dipole-forbidden $5s$ $^2S_{1/2}$ $\rightarrow$ $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ transition in $^{88}$Sr$^+$ was driven, partially resolving the Zeeman structure and yielding a Gaussian linewidth of 14.5(8) MHz, with the residual width attributed to the ions' micromotion. The lifetime of the metastable $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ state was measured to be 0.325(5)$_{\mathrm{stat}}$(4)$_{\mathrm{sys}}$ s, uncorrected for collisional quenching. Several measurements to quantify the cooling timescale, the detection rate of the photon collection region and the trap storage lifetime were also performed. The developed technique will allow radioactive ion beams to be decelerated and cooled for precision spectroscopy measurements.

title: What constrains the neutron-star crust? Present data, future measurements, and EOS doppelg\"angers
abstract: The neutron-star crust plays a central role in pulsar glitches, thermal evolution, and stellar oscillations, yet its properties remain difficult to constrain. We use Bayesian inference with a unified crust-core equation of state to assess what present nuclear and astrophysical data tell us about the crust and what future stellar measurements can add. Within this model, present crust constraints are dominated by chiral effective field theory, with laboratory data providing additional information and current stellar observations having a smaller effect. The adopted theoretical bands determine how tightly the crust properties are constrained, while the treatment of neutron-rich surface energy affects their inferred values. Forecasts centred on a single reference equation of state show that more precise measurements of radius, tidal deformability, and total moment of inertia mainly constrain crust thickness. They provide little additional information about the crust-core transition, crust mass, or crustal moment of inertia and do not recover the precision lost when the chiral effective field theory constraint is removed. Two models with nearly identical global stellar observables can have crust masses and crustal moments of inertia differing by about a factor of two, yet remain indistinguishable at the assumed precision. Precise global measurements therefore need not uniquely determine the crust. Observations that directly probe the crust are needed to distinguish these models.

title: Waveform-based pulse timing enhanced by self-supervised neural regression models for digital nuclear instrumentation
abstract: With the rapid development of high-sampling-rate digital nuclear devices, their applications in nuclear facilities and related fields become more acceptable, and will possibly become widespread due to the versatility and flexibility of waveform sampling systems. When digitizers reach hundreds of megahertz or gigahertz, their lower limit in time measurement probes into the sub-nanosecond region, expediting their use in a bunch of time-critical scenarios. While conventional algorithms coupled with digital sampling techniques realize fair pulse timing in certain conditions, the potentials are still open to compact and efficient machine learning models. In this paper, we intend to boost the performance of pulse timing with a new paradigm of self-supervised learning on matched waveform pairs. The proposed method combines the mainstream self-supervised loss and the auxiliary weakly-supervised loss on the reference set, jointly improving the timing performance. We apply the method in a gamma/neutron-mixed radiation field, common in nuclear facilities. The simulation and experimental results show that, the proposed method not only outperforms conventional timing algorithms, but also surpasses neural network models based on supervised learning alone. Considering the trained model is lightweight and computationally efficient, it is promising to deploy it on edge devices, like economical microcontrollers with neural processing units.

title: Two-nucleon scattering amplitudes at light quark masses from lattice QCD
abstract: We present a lattice-QCD determination of nucleon-nucleon scattering amplitudes at pion masses of $M_\pi \approx 200$ MeV and $M_\pi \approx 280$ MeV at a single lattice spacing $a \approx 0.064$ fm on two CLS ensembles. The finite-volume energy spectra are extracted from large Hermitian correlation matrices constructed within the distillation framework using an extensive basis of two-nucleon interpolating operators. To reliably relate the finite-volume spectra to the infinite-volume scattering amplitudes, we employ two recently developed formalisms that explicitly account for the long-range interaction generated by one-pion exchange: the plane-wave quantization condition and the relativistic left-hand-cut formalism. We discuss the quark-mass dependence of the nucleon-nucleon scattering lengths, effective ranges, shape parameters and pole positions. At all pion masses considered, our analysis prefers virtual states in both isospin channels by more than $1\sigma$. Comparing also results from our previous calculation at $M_\pi \approx 710$ MeV, we observe that the inverse scattering lengths and binding momenta approach their physical-point phenomenological values monotonically as the pion mass is varied.

At all pion masses considered, our analysis prefers virtual states in both isospin channels by more than $1\sigma$. title: The inclination cross-check: binary-pulsar timing and gravitational-wave polarimetry
abstract: Radio timing and gravitational-wave (GW) polarimetry provide independent measurements of a binary's inclination. We study their consistency through $\eps=s_{\rm Shapiro}-s_{\rm GW}$, where $s_{\rm Shapiro}$ is the Shapiro-delay shape and $s_{\rm GW}$ is inferred from the tensor polarization amplitudes. We combine a time-dependent, finite-arm detector response with radio timing averaged over each integration, retaining the amplitude--inclination covariance and the nonlinear orientation posteriors. For hypothetical 15-minute binaries at 5 kpc and $65^\circ$ inclination, four years of GW data and a 125-h radio campaign give $\sigma_\eps=5.4\times10^{-3}$ for a double neutron star and $1.0\times10^{-3}$ for a pulsar--black-hole binary when two static timing harmonics are fitted. An apsidally evolving radio model with $e=0.01$ and a free apsidal rate gives $4.5\times10^{-3}$ and $0.94\times10^{-3}$, respectively, with the circular GW covariance held fixed. Changes in the relative tensor amplitudes can be absorbed by the GW fit as an apparent inclination shift and revealed by the radio measurement. An inaccurate detector response can produce a similar discrepancy even when its Fisher errors are nearly unchanged. These forecasts use the $n=2$ GW harmonic and assume a fixed orbital plane, sustained radio visibility, and the specified timing precision; additional harmonics can provide further orientation information.

title: Study of neutron flux redistribution and shadowing effect in rod worth measurements with the rod drop experiment
abstract: This study investigates neutron flux redistribution and the shadowing effect between control rods during rod-worth measurements using the rod-drop experiment. A simulation-based instrumental calibration methodology is proposed to account for spatial effects on neutron detector responses and improve the accuracy of reactivity measurements. The IPEN/MB-01 research reactor was modeled using the MCNP Monte Carlo neutron transport code. Reactivity behavior during the initial transient of the rod-drop experiment (t < 10 s) was evaluated and compared with experimental measurements using the source-jerk method. The methodology quantifies control rod shadowing and detector-dependent neutron flux redistribution, allowing correction factors to be established for the measured reactivity. Control-bank worth values obtained through the stable-period method were adopted as reference measurements. The reported maximum deviations from the reference values were 0.5% and 11.3%, respectively. The results demonstrate the relevance of spatial neutron flux effects, control rod interactions, and detector calibration in rod-drop experiments, providing a computational and experimental basis for improving control rod worth measurements in research reactors.

title: Rank-One Ultralight Dark Matter Response in a Full-Tensor Gravity Gradiometer
abstract: A full-tensor superconducting gravity gradiometer whose four test masses carry two compositions in a $2+2$ pattern acquires a composition-dependent channel for dilaton-coupled ultralight dark matter. The reconstructed response is the rank-one tensor $\K=\gv_\phi(t)\otimes\qv$, with the axis of $\qv$ fixed in advance by the material assignment, and obeys the parameter-free null condition $\K(\mathbf{I}-\Pq)=0$, which no gravity gradient or platform rotation alone can satisfy; it vanishes for a single composition. For copper and lead, the sensitivity reaches $d_{\hat m}-d_g\simeq3.4\times10^{-8}$, and $4.9\times10^{-10}$ with upgraded accelerometers.

title: Projected sensitivity to light WIMP-like particles of the BULLKID-DM experiment
abstract: BULLKID-DM is an experiment designed for the direct searches of particle dark matter candidates with mass around 1 GeV, or below, and cross-section with nucleons smaller than $10^{-40}$ cm$^2$. The detector consists of a stack of diced silicon wafers, acting as arrays of particle absorbers, sensed by multiplexed Kinetic Inductance Detectors. The target will amount to 800 g subdivided in more than 2000 silicon dice, with the aim of controlling the background from natural radioactivity by creating a fully active structure and by applying fiducialization techniques. In this work we present the projected sensitivity of BULLKID-DM to light WIMP-like particles considering also the other future experiments in the field.

title: Observation of Non-Equilibrium Phonon Loss Across a Solid-Superfluid Interface
abstract: We measure the performance of an athermal phonon calorimeter in vacuum and in thermal contact with superfluid $^4$He. Using a cryogenic photon calibration system, we show that the superfluid suppresses the collection of the phonon signal by over 99\%. We conclude that submerged sensors will not benefit TESSERACT's superfluid helium dark matter target, but that superfluid helium may be useful to superconducting qubits as a sink for athermal phonons generated by radiation and other spontaneous sources. Our measurement is the first probe of solid-to-superfluid phonon transmission at energies higher than those stably supportable by the superfluid. We discuss thermal flow inside the calorimeter, as well as systematics from an alternative calibration scheme.

title: Feasibility study of light sterile neutrino searches with a future NINJA-like detector
abstract:
In this paper, we investigate the sensitivity of future NINJA-like experiment at J-PARC to eV-scale sterile neutrinos within the 3+1 framework. We perform a phenomenological feasibility study using the $
u_\mu ightarrow 
u_e$ appearance, $
u_\mu ightarrow 
u_\mu$ and $
u_e ightarrow 
u_e$ disappearance channels, focusing on possible future configurations of the detector located at different floors of the NM building (B2, SS, and GROUND), corresponding to different off-axis angles. Our analysis is based on a simplified and effective detector response, in which events are classified into electron-like and muon-like topologies and constant benchmark selection efficiencies are applied. We explore different exposure scenarios and assess the impact of analysis choices such as upper energy cuts. We include systematic uncertainties corresponding to normalization for signal and background rates and study the robustness of our results with respect to variations in the assumed energy resolution, and vary efficiencies for key backgrounds such as muon misidentification from charge current and neutral current interactions. Finally, we examine the effects of combining data from multiple detector locations. We find that the SS floor provides the strongest constraints on the active-sterile mixing parameters, while the B2 and GROUND configurations offer constraints comparable to the current bounds for probed mass-squared differences. Our results indicate that a NINJA-like detector, optimized for sufficient statistics and benchmark identification performance, has the potential to provide competitive constraints on light sterile neutrino scenarios in its future runs.
